title: Time Series Analysis Part 1: Exercise 1
text:
Question 1: The forecasting process (15)
Context: producing sales forecasts for several products of a large biscuit manufacturer.
1. Problem definition. The aim is to forecast future sales for the company’s range of biscuits so that it can make strategic and operational decisions about how, when and where to sell and produce. This means pinning down exactly what is forecast: which products (individual biscuit lines or product families), at what level (national, regional or by retailer), in what units, how far ahead and how often (e.g. weekly forecasts for production scheduling, monthly forecasts a year ahead for ingredient purchasing and budgeting). This is done by talking to the people who will use the forecasts (production, procurement, sales and marketing, finance).
2. Data collection. For each product, collect a record of how many units were sold each period (e.g. monthly), building up a historical time series that can be used to forecast future sales. Also collect information on factors that help explain sales: prices, promotions, advertising campaigns, product launches and competitor activity, along with calendar effects such as public holidays, school holidays and weekends. Knowledge from the sales team about one-off events (stock-outs, factory shutdowns, a large once-off order) is also recorded so the data can be interpreted correctly.
3. Data analysis. This is the exploratory stage, done before any model is fitted. Plot each series and look for trend, seasonality (e.g. peaks before Christmas and Easter), cycles, outliers and structural breaks; check whether a transformation (e.g. logs) or differencing is needed; examine the ACF/PACF; and look at how sales relate to drivers such as promotions, in order to understand consumer demand at different times of the year. The arrow back from model selection shows the process is iterative: what is learnt when fitting a model can send us back to look at the data again.
4. Model selection and fitting. Based on the patterns found in the data analysis (and the ACF and PACF, which show the autocorrelation structure), choose candidate models, e.g. exponential smoothing (such as Holt–Winters for trending, seasonal products), ARIMA/seasonal ARIMA, state space models, or regression models with promotion and price effects, and estimate their parameters on the historical data.
5. Model validation. Assess how accurate each model’s forecasts are. Split the data so that a hold-out (test) set is kept back, and compare forecasts with the actual values using metrics such as RMSE, MAE and MAPE, using validation approaches such as rolling-origin (time series cross-validation) or sliding windows. Residuals should also be checked to make sure they look like white noise. The best-performing model is chosen.
6. Forecasting model deployment. Put the forecasts into practical use, since the whole point of forecasting is to support decisions. The chosen model is built into the company’s planning systems and produces forecasts (with prediction intervals) on a regular schedule, which are used for decisions such as production planning, which products to invest in or refine, and advertising strategies targeted at the products and times of year where sales are strongest.
7. Monitoring forecasting model performance. Continuously compare forecasts with actual sales as they come in and track the forecast errors over time, to detect bias or deterioration, for instance when consumer preferences change or a competitor changes strategy. This monitoring could be automated (e.g. an automated system or AI agent that is fed new data, updates the forecasts and flags when errors drift or market changes occur). When performance deteriorates, the model is re-estimated or the process returns to an earlier stage.

title: Time Series Analysis Part 1: Exercise 1
text:
Question 2: Expected time patterns (8)
(a) Monthly sales of computer hard drives at a local store (10 years). Over the 10 years I would expect a trend: sales would initially increase steadily as computers became more common and people bought hard drives to keep their computers going for longer, but then trend downwards as technology develops and newer products (e.g. solid-state drives and cloud storage) replace them. There would also be seasonality within each year, e.g. at the beginning of the year when school and university go back, and around Black Friday and the festive season. (Because the data are monthly, within-month effects such as payday are not visible.)
(b) Hourly pulse rate of a person for one week. A strong daily (24-hour) seasonal pattern: pulse rate is elevated during the day while the person is moving around and active, and drops to a resting level while they sleep at night. If the person exercises every day, there will also be a regular daily spike in heart rate at that time. Little or no trend would be expected over a single week.
(c) Daily sales at a fast-food store for six months. A weekly seasonal pattern, with increased demand and sales over weekends (Friday nights to Sunday), plus increases around public holidays (and possibly month-end/payday). Six months is quite a short period, so long-term trends would be hard to see.
(d) Weekly electricity consumption for your local area (10 years). A strong annual seasonal pattern: in South Africa consumption is highest in winter (heating, longer nights) with a possible smaller summer peak from air-conditioning, and dips over the December holidays when businesses and industry shut down. There would also be a trend reflecting population growth and development, possibly offset in recent years by load-shedding, higher tariffs and rooftop solar.

title: Time Series Analysis Part 1: Exercise 1
text:
Question 3: Matching series to ACFs (12)
The key idea is: a trend makes neighbouring values (even ones far apart) similar, so the ACF starts very high and decays slowly while staying positive; seasonality/cycles make the ACF oscillate, with peaks at lags equal to the period; and a series with neither has small autocorrelations that die out quickly.

Matching each series to its ACF







Time series
ACF
Reason




1. Daily morning temperature of a cow
B
No seasonality or strong trend, just a slight downward drift and irregular variation. The ACF has small-to-moderate positive values that die out without any regular oscillation, consistent with a weakly persistent, non-seasonal series.


2. Accidental deaths in USA (monthly)
A
Clear monthly seasonality with period 12 and no trend. ACF A has a large positive spike at lag 12 and strong negative values around lag 6 (half a seasonal cycle), the pattern of a period-12 seasonal series.


3. International airline passengers
D
Strong upward trend plus seasonality. The trend produces very large positive autocorrelations that decay slowly (ACF D starts near 0.9 and stays high); the seasonality shows as a small bump around lag 12.


4. Annual mink trappings (Canada)
C
An annual series with a regular population cycle of roughly 10 years. ACF C oscillates with peaks near lags 10 and 20 and troughs near lags 5 and 15, matching a ~10-year cycle.

Question 5: Souvenir shop sales (20)


Show code

names(souv)[1] <- "Month"
souv_ts <- ts(as.vector(as.matrix(souv[, -1])), start = c(1987, 1), frequency = 12)



(a) Time plot and description (4)

Time plotSeasonal plot




Show code

  labs(x = "Year", y = "Sales")








Figure 2: Monthly sales of the souvenir shop, January 1987 – December 1993.









Show code
ggseasonplot(souv_ts, year.labels = TRUE) + labs(title = NULL, y = "Sales")








Figure 3: Seasonal plot: each line is one year.









Trend: sales increase strongly over time, consistent with the shop expanding its premises, products and staff. The growth accelerates in 1992–1993.
Seasonality: a very strong annual pattern. Sales build up through November and peak sharply every December (Christmas tourists), then drop back in January. A smaller secondary peak occurs each March from 1988 onward (the surf festival). There is no March peak in 1987 because the festival only started in 1988.
Changing variance: the size of the seasonal fluctuations grows with the level of the series (the December peaks become enormous), so the seasonality is multiplicative rather than additive.
Unusual features: sales in 1990–1991 stalled: December 1990 (30114) was below December 1989 (34061), and January and March 1991 were lower than a year earlier, breaking the upward trend (possibly an economic downturn or poor tourist season). There are also some months that deviate from the usual seasonal shape, e.g. the unusually high March 1990 and the very sharp jump in December 1992 and 1993.



(b) Why take logarithms? (2)
The variance of the series increases with its level: the seasonal swings are proportional to the level (multiplicative seasonality). Most models (and linear regression) assume constant variance and additive components. Taking logarithms stabilises the variance and turns multiplicative effects into additive ones (\(\log(T \times S \times E) = \log T + \log S + \log E\)), and turns exponential growth into a linear trend (Figure 4).


Show code
autoplot(log(souv_ts)) + labs(x = "Year", y = "log(Sales)")








Figure 4: Log of monthly sales; the seasonal swings are now roughly constant in size.

title: Time Series Analysis Part 1: Exercise 1
text:
Question 6: IBM daily closing prices (4)

Time plot: the series does not fluctuate around a constant mean. It wanders up from about 450 to 600, then falls sharply to about 300–400, with long local “trends”. There is no level to which it reverts, which is typical of a random walk.
ACF: the autocorrelations start close to 1 and decay extremely slowly (still about 0.8 at lag 25). For a stationary series the ACF should drop to zero quickly; a slowly decaying ACF is the classic sign of non-stationarity.
PACF: there is a single very large spike at lag 1 of almost exactly 1, with all other partial autocorrelations negligible. This indicates \(Y_t \approx Y_{t-1} + e_t\), i.e. an AR(1) with \(\phi_1 \approx 1\), i.e. a unit root.

Together these show the series is non-stationary and should be differenced (first differences \(Y_t - Y_{t-1}\), i.e. the daily price changes, are likely to be stationary).

title: Time Series Analysis Part 1: Exercise 1
text:
Question 7: Strikes in the USA, 1951–1980 (16)


Show code
strikes_raw <- read_excel(data_file, sheet = 3, .name_repair = "minimal")
strikes <- ts(c(strikes_raw[[2]], strikes_raw[[5]]), start = 1951)



(a) Why ARIMA(0,1,1)? (3)

Original seriesFirst differences




Show code
ggtsdisplay(strikes, main = "Number of strikes", xlab = "Year")








Figure 6: Strikes series: time plot, ACF and PACF.









Show code
ggtsdisplay(diff(strikes), main = "Differenced number of strikes", xlab = "Year")








Figure 7: First differences of the strikes series: time plot, ACF and PACF.









The original series (Figure 6) wanders: it falls from about 5 000 in the early 1950s to about 3 400 in the early 1960s, then rises to around 6 000 in the 1970s, without reverting to a fixed mean. The ACF decays slowly (0.73 at lag 1 and still positive for several lags), and the PACF has one large spike at lag 1. The series is non-stationary, so it should be differenced once (\(d = 1\)).
The differenced series (Figure 7) fluctuates around a constant mean of about zero with roughly constant variance, so it appears stationary. Its ACF has a single negative spike at lag 1 (-0.34, close to the \(\pm 2/\sqrt{n} \approx \pm 0.37\) bound) and is negligible thereafter (the ACF “cuts off” after lag 1), while the PACF decays. This is the signature of an MA(1) process for the differences (\(q = 1\), \(p = 0\)).

Hence ARIMA(0,1,1) is appropriate. (No constant is included since the differences have mean approximately zero, so there is no persistent trend in the series.)


(b) Backshift operator form (2)
With \(B Y_t = Y_{t-1}\), the ARIMA(0,1,1) model is \[(1 - B)\,Y_t = (1 + \theta_1 B)\, e_t \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad Y_t = Y_{t-1} + e_t + \theta_1 e_{t-1},\] where \(e_t\) is white noise.






Tip



R uses the “\(+\theta\)” sign convention; some textbooks write \((1 - \theta_1 B)e_t\), in which case the sign of the estimate is reversed.




(c) Fit the model and examine the residuals (5)


Show code
fit_strikes <- Arima(strikes, order = c(0, 1, 1))
fit_strikes

The fitted model is \[(1 - B)\,Y_t = (1 -0.3094\,B)\,e_t, \qquad \hat\sigma^2 = 330 817.\]


Show code

Figure 8: Residual diagnostics for the ARIMA(0,1,1) model.






The time plot of residuals shows no pattern and fluctuates around zero with roughly constant variance.
All residual autocorrelations lie within the significance bounds, so no autocorrelation remains.
The histogram is roughly symmetric and consistent with normality (given only 29 residuals).
The Ljung–Box test gives \(Q^* = 4.258\) on 9 df, p-value \(= 0.894\), so we do not reject the null hypothesis that the residuals are white noise.

The model is therefore satisfactory: the residuals behave like white noise, so the model has captured the structure in the data (Figure 8).


(d) Forecasts three steps ahead by hand (4)
From \(Y_t = Y_{t-1} + e_t + \theta_1 e_{t-1}\), the forecasts made at origin \(n = 1980\) are \[\hat{Y}_{n+1} = Y_n + \hat\theta_1\, e_n, \qquad \hat{Y}_{n+h} = \hat{Y}_{n+h-1} \;\;(h \ge 2),\] because future errors have expectation zero. So all three forecasts are equal.


Show code

e_n <- tail(residuals(fit_strikes), 1)
f1 <- y_n + theta * e_n


With \(Y_{1980} = 3885\), the last residual \(e_{1980} = -880.24\), and \(\hat\theta_1 = -0.3094\): \[\hat{Y}_{1981} = 3885 + (-0.3094)(-880.24) = 4157.33,\] \[\hat{Y}_{1982} = \hat{Y}_{1983} = 4157.33.\]

title: Time Series Analysis Part 1: Exercise 1
text:
Question 8: Bituminous coal production (10)

(a) What sort of ARIMA model? (3)
The model \(Y_t = c + \phi_1 Y_{t-1} + \phi_2 Y_{t-2} + \phi_3 Y_{t-3} + \phi_4 Y_{t-4} + e_t\) is an autoregressive model of order 4 on the undifferenced series with no moving-average terms: an ARIMA(4,0,0), i.e. AR(4), with \(p = 4\), \(d = 0\), \(q = 0\).


(b) Why was this model chosen? (1)
The time plot fluctuates around a fairly constant mean (roughly 300–630 million tons, no persistent trend) and the ACF dies down quickly, so the series appears stationary and no differencing is needed (\(d=0\)). The ACF decays in a damped, sine-wave-like fashion (typical of an AR process), while the PACF has significant spikes at lags 1 and 4 and cuts off after lag 4, which identifies an AR(4) model.


(c) Forecasts for 1969–1971 (6)


Show code
c0  <- 146.1
phi <- c(0.891, -0.257, 0.392, -0.333)
coal <- c(`1964` = 467, `1965` = 512, `1966` = 534, `1967` = 552, `1968` = 545)

Y <- coal
for (h in 1:3) {
  n <- length(Y)
  Y <- c(Y, c0 + sum(phi * Y[n:(n - 3)]))   # uses Y_{t-1}, ..., Y_{t-4}
}
coal_fc <- tail(Y, 3)


Future errors are set to zero and forecasts are substituted for unknown future values:
\[
\begin{aligned}

text:
NoteExecutive summary



Title: State space models for South African accommodation demand
Section and topic: Section 2. Linear Gaussian state space models: the Kalman filter, maximum likelihood through the prediction error decomposition, the Kalman state and disturbance smoothers, forecasting, structural time series models and missing observations.
Type of project: Implementation from first principles on real-world data, with a simulation study and a model comparison.
Question: What do the four operations of a state space model (filtering, likelihood, smoothing and prediction) tell us about monthly accommodation demand in South Africa, when the 25 COVID-19 months are treated as missing? Specifically: how does the filter track demand in real time and through the gap, how well do the data determine the model, how much demand was lost to COVID-19, and do the forecasts beat the Project 1 SARIMA and the Project 3 exponential smoothing models?
Data: Real-world, publicly available data from Statistics South Africa, Tourist Accommodation release P6410, series B64100 (stay unit nights sold, total industry, thousands), monthly, January 2015 to June 2026. Source details are in Section 2.
Methods: I write my own Kalman filter (with missing observations), log likelihood, state and disturbance smoothers and forecasting functions, and check them on the accommodation series itself: against the base R Kalman routines, and by reproducing the exact log likelihood of the Project 1 SARIMA. Four structural models are estimated by maximum likelihood and compared by AIC, profile likelihoods and innovation diagnostics. The filter is used to follow demand month by month through the gap and the restart, the smoothers to estimate the demand lost to COVID-19 and to flag unusual months, and a simulation study from the fitted model checks whether the lost-demand estimate and its uncertainty can be trusted. Forecasts are evaluated on the same test set as Projects 1 and 3 and by rolling-origin cross-validation.
Key findings: See Section 11.1.
What I would do differently: Use the exact diffuse initialisation, add the Project 3 intervention terms and an Easter regressor to the state space model, and model the post-COVID period with its own variances.
Detailed analysis: the sections below.

title: Project 4: State Space Models for South African Accommodation Demand
section: 3.1 The model and what each part means
text:
3.1 The model and what each part means
Write \(y_t = \log(\text{nights sold}_t)\). The simplest model that matches Figure 1 is a local level plus seasonal model:
\[
\begin{aligned}
y_t &= \mu_t + \gamma_t + \varepsilon_t, & \varepsilon_t &\sim N(0, \sigma^2_\varepsilon), \\
\mu_{t+1} &= \mu_t + \xi_t, & \xi_t &\sim N(0, \sigma^2_\xi), \\
\gamma_{t+1} &= -\textstyle\sum_{j=0}^{10} \gamma_{t-j} + \omega_t, & \omega_t &\sim N(0, \sigma^2_\omega).
\end{aligned}
\]
In words:

\(\mu_t\) is the underlying level of demand: log nights sold with the calendar effect removed. A level shock \(\xi_t\) is a permanent change in demand, such as a new air route, a visa rule or the post-COVID reset.
\(\gamma_t\) is the seasonal effect of the calendar month (December high, winter months low). The twelve effects sum to roughly zero over a year, and the shock \(\omega_t\) lets the pattern change slowly, for example if school holidays move or the mix of business and leisure travel changes.
\(\varepsilon_t\) is month-specific noise that does not persist, such as the timing of Easter or a large conference.

The three variances decide how the filter interprets a surprise: is a month with unexpectedly high sales a sign that demand has moved up for good (level), that the seasonal pattern has changed (seasonal), or a one-off (irregular)? Estimating them is the job of the likelihood.

title: Project 4: State Space Models for South African Accommodation Demand
text:
3.2 State space form
Any linear Gaussian state space model can be written as (Durbin and Koopman, 2012)
\[
y_t = Z^\top \alpha_t + \varepsilon_t, \quad \varepsilon_t \sim N(0, H), \qquad
\alpha_{t+1} = T \alpha_t + R \eta_t, \quad \eta_t \sim N(0, Q), \qquad \alpha_1 \sim N(a_1, P_1).
\]
For the model above the state vector holds the level and the current and previous ten seasonal effects, \(\alpha_t = (\mu_t, \gamma_t, \gamma_{t-1}, \dots, \gamma_{t-10})^\top\), so \(m = 12\), and
\[
Z = (1, 1, 0, \dots, 0)^\top, \quad
T = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & T_\gamma \end{pmatrix}, \quad
T_\gamma = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & -1 & \cdots & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & \cdots & 0 & 0 \\ \vdots & & \ddots & & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & \cdots & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad
H = \sigma^2_\varepsilon, \quad Q = \text{diag}(\sigma^2_\xi, \sigma^2_\omega),
\]
with \(R\) the \(12 \times 2\) matrix that sends \(\xi_t\) to the level and \(\omega_t\) to the current seasonal effect. The other three candidate models (Section 4.1) only change these matrices; the code that filters, smooths and forecasts never changes.

title: Project 4: State Space Models for South African Accommodation Demand
text:
3.3 Filtering, likelihood, smoothing and prediction
Filter. Let \(a_t\) and \(P_t\) be the mean and variance of the state given the data up to month \(t-1\). For each month the filter computes
\[
v_t = y_t - Z^\top a_t, \quad F_t = Z^\top P_t Z + H, \quad K_t = T P_t Z / F_t, \quad
a_{t+1} = T a_t + K_t v_t, \quad P_{t+1} = T P_t T^\top - K_t K_t^\top F_t + R Q R^\top .
\]
\(v_t\) is the forecast error for month \(t\) made at the end of month \(t-1\) (the innovation), \(F_t\) its variance, and the Kalman gain \(K_t\) says how the surprise is shared out between the level and the seasonal effects. If month \(t\) is missing (a COVID month) there is nothing to learn, so \(a_{t+1} = T a_t\) and \(P_{t+1} = T P_t T^\top + R Q R^\top\): the filter carries its last view of demand forward and becomes less certain every month.
Likelihood. The innovations are independent, so the log likelihood is the prediction error decomposition
\[
\log L = -\tfrac{1}{2} \textstyle\sum_{t} \left( \log 2\pi + \log F_t + v_t^2 / F_t \right),
\]
summed over the observed months only: the COVID months contribute nothing. The initial level and seasonal effects are unknown, so I use a diffuse prior, \(a_1 = 0\) and \(P_1 = \kappa I\) with \(\kappa = 10^7\), and leave the first \(d = 13\) innovations out of the likelihood, since they only serve to learn the starting values (the large-\(\kappa\) approximation to the exact diffuse filter, Durbin and Koopman, 2012, Chapter 5).
Smoothers. Working backwards from \(r_n = 0\), \(N_n = 0\) with \(L_t = T - K_t Z^\top\),
\[
r_{t-1} = Z v_t / F_t + L_t^\top r_t, \qquad N_{t-1} = Z Z^\top / F_t + L_t^\top N_t L_t,
\]
(with \(r_{t-1} = T^\top r_t\) and \(N_{t-1} = T^\top N_t T\) for a missing month), the smoothed state is \(\hat\alpha_t = a_t + P_t r_{t-1}\) with variance \(V_t = P_t - P_t N_{t-1} P_t\). The disturbance smoother gives the smoothed state shocks \(\hat\eta_t = Q R^\top r_t\) with variance \(Q - Q R^\top N_t R Q\) (Durbin and Koopman, 2012, Section 4.5). Standardised, these auxiliary residuals are \(t\)-statistics for a break in the level or the seasonal pattern at month \(t\).
Prediction. Forecasting is filtering with every future month missing: the \(h\)-step forecast of \(y\) is \(Z^\top a\) with variance \(Z^\top P Z + H\), where \(a\) and \(P\) are propagated with the missing-month recursion.

The damped trend model is the state space counterpart of the damped Holt–Winters method that did best in Project 3, and the level + seasonal model corresponds to ETS(A,N,A). The AR(1) component allows deviations from the trend that last a few months, such as a slow recovery after a shock.


Code
# Build the system matrices for one of the structural models ------------------
# trend: "llt" (local linear trend), "ll" (local level), "damped"
param_names <- function(trend, ar) {
  c("eps", "level", if (trend != "ll") "slope", "seas",
    if (trend == "damped") "phi", if (ar) c("ar_var", "rho"))
}

unpack <- function(theta, trend, ar) {
  nm <- param_names(trend, ar)
  p  <- as.list(exp(theta)); names(p) <- nm
  if (trend == "damped") p$phi <- 0.98 * plogis(theta[nm == "phi"])   # phi in (0, 0.98)
  if (ar)                p$rho <- tanh(theta[nm == "rho"])             # rho in (-1, 1)
  if (trend == "ll")     p$slope <- NA
  p
}

structural_sys <- function(p, trend, ar) {
  n_tr <- if (trend == "ll") 1 else 2
  m <- n_tr + 11 + ar
  Tm <- matrix(0, m, m); Z <- numeric(m)
  Tm[1, 1] <- 1; Z[1] <- 1                                  # level
  if (n_tr == 2) {                                          # slope
    Tm[1, 2] <- 1
    Tm[2, 2] <- if (trend == "damped") p$phi else 1
  }
  s1 <- n_tr + 1                                            # seasonal block (11 states)
  Tm[s1, s1:(s1 + 10)] <- -1
  Tm[(s1 + 1):(s1 + 10), s1:(s1 + 9)] <- diag(10)
  Z[s1] <- 1
  if (ar) { Tm[m, m] <- p$rho; Z[m] <- 1 }                  # AR(1) component
  shock_rows <- c(1, if (n_tr == 2) 2, s1, if (ar) m)
  shock_var  <- c(p$level, if (n_tr == 2) p$slope, p$seas, if (ar) p$ar_var)
  R <- matrix(0, m, length(shock_rows))
  R[cbind(shock_rows, seq_along(shock_rows))] <- 1
  P1 <- diag(1e7, m)                                        # diffuse prior
  if (ar) P1[m, m] <- p$ar_var / (1 - p$rho^2)              # stationary prior for c_t
  list(Z = matrix(Z), H = p$eps, T = Tm, R = R,
       Q = diag(shock_var, length(shock_var)), a1 = rep(0, m), P1 = P1)
}

d_diffuse <- 13   # same number of dropped innovations for every model, so AIC is comparable

ssm_negll <- function(theta, y, trend, ar) {
  -kloglik(kfilter(y, structural_sys(unpack(theta, trend, ar), trend, ar)), d = d_diffuse)
}

# Maximum likelihood with several starting values (the surface is flat near the boundary)
fit_structural <- function(y, trend, ar, start = NULL) {
  nm <- param_names(trend, ar)
  th0 <- c(eps = log(1e-3), level = log(1e-3), slope = log(1e-5), seas = log(1e-5),
           phi = qlogis(0.9 / 0.98), ar_var = log(1e-3), rho = atanh(0.5))[nm]
  starts <- if (is.null(start)) list(th0, th0 + 0.5, th0 - 1) else list(start)
  best <- NULL
  for (s in starts) {
    o <- optim(s, ssm_negll, y = y, trend = trend, ar = ar, method = "BFGS",
               control = list(maxit = 500))
    o <- optim(o$par, ssm_negll, y = y, trend = trend, ar = ar, method = "Nelder-Mead",
               control = list(maxit = 4000))
    if (is.null(best) || o$value < best$value) best <- o
  }
  p   <- unpack(best$par, trend, ar)
  sys <- structural_sys(p, trend, ar)
  kf  <- kfilter(y, sys)
  list(theta = best$par, p = p, sys = sys, kf = kf, loglik = -best$value,
       k = length(nm), trend = trend, ar = ar, converged = best$convergence == 0)
}

What the estimates say about accommodation demand (Table 2):

There is almost no month-specific noise. The irregular variance is essentially zero in every model, so the filter treats nearly every surprise as either a permanent change in demand or a change in the seasonal pattern. On the log scale, demand behaves like a random-walk level plus a slowly evolving seasonal pattern.
The level moves; the growth rate does not. In the level + seasonal model the level variance is 4.5e-04, a monthly standard deviation of 2.1% in underlying demand. In the BSM the slope variance is 9.8e-11, so the growth rate is effectively a fixed drift.
The seasonal pattern changes slowly. The seasonal variance is about a fifth of the level variance: each month’s seasonal effect drifts by roughly 0.9% a month.
Damping and AR(1). The damped trend model estimates \(\phi\) = 0.901, and the AR(1) component raises the log likelihood by only 0.10 for two extra parameters.
Model selection. The lowest AIC belongs to the Level + seasonal model, which I use for the filtering and smoothing analysis below. The AIC values span only a few units, so the data do not strongly distinguish between the trend specifications: with the growth rate barely moving, adding a slope buys almost nothing in one-step fit. Its effect shows up in long-horizon forecasts instead (Section 9).

section: 5.2 Checking my code on the accommodation series
text:
5.2 Checking my code on the accommodation series
Before interpreting the filter and smoother, I check that my code computes the right quantities on this series, missing months included. I use two independent references.
1. The base R Kalman routines. stats::KalmanLike() and stats::KalmanRun() implement the same filter in C. I give them exactly the system matrices of the fitted Level + seasonal model and the series with the COVID months as NA.


Code
mod_r <- list(T = sel$sys$T, Z = as.numeric(sel$sys$Z), h = sel$sys$H,
              V = sel$sys$R %*% sel$sys$Q %*% t(sel$sys$R),
              a = sel$sys$a1, P = sel$sys$P1, Pn = sel$sys$P1)
kl <- stats::KalmanLike(y_tour, mod_r, nit = 0L)
kr <- stats::KalmanRun(y_tour, mod_r, nit = 0L)

# KalmanLike reports 0.5 * (log(s2) + mean(log F)) with s2 = mean(v^2 / F), over all observed months
ok_all  <- which(!is.na(sel_kf$v))
my_s2   <- mean(sel_kf$v[ok_all]^2 / sel_kf$F[ok_all])
my_Lik  <- 0.5 * (log(my_s2) + mean(log(sel_kf$F[ok_all])))
# KalmanRun returns the filtered states a_{t|t} and standardised innovations
att <- t(sapply(seq_len(n_tr), function(t)
  if (is.na(y_tour[t])) sel_kf$a[t, ] else
    sel_kf$a[t, ] + sel_kf$P[, , t] %*% sel$sys$Z * sel_kf$v[t] / sel_kf$F[t]))
diff_state <- max(abs(kr$states - att))
diff_innov <- max(abs(kr$resid - sel_kf$v / sqrt(sel_kf$F)), na.rm = TRUE)


The two implementations agree: the likelihood summary is -1.861978 from my code and -1.861978 from KalmanLike(), the largest difference in the filtered states over all 114 months (including the 25 missing ones) is 1.4e-07, and in the standardised innovations 6.9e-06.
2. Reproducing the Project 1 SARIMA likelihood. Project 1’s SARIMA(0,1,1)(0,1,1)12 (the “airline” model) was fitted to the same log series with the same months missing; R evaluates its likelihood with a Kalman filter. The ARIMA model can be put in state space form (stats::makeARIMA() builds \(Z\), \(T\), \(R\), \(Q\) and the diffuse \(P_1\) for the 14 differencing and MA states). If my filter is correct, running it on those matrices must give exactly the log likelihood that arima() reports. I also maximise the likelihood myself, using my filter, to see whether I get the same estimates.


Code
y_ts <- ts(y_tour, start = c(2015, 1), frequency = 12)
fit_airline <- arima(y_ts, order = c(0, 1, 1),
                     seasonal = list(order = c(0, 1, 1), period = 12), method = "ML")

airline_sys <- function(ma, sma, s2) {
  theta <- c(ma, rep(0, 10), sma, ma * sma)               # (1 + theta B)(1 + Theta B^12)
  Delta <- c(1, rep(0, 10), 1, -1)                         # (1 - B)(1 - B^12)
  mk <- makeARIMA(numeric(0), theta, Delta, kappa = 1e6)
  m  <- length(mk$a)
  list(Z = matrix(mk$Z), H = 0, T = mk$T, R = diag(m), Q = mk$V * s2,
       a1 = mk$a, P1 = mk$Pn * s2, s2 = s2)
}
# arima() leaves out the diffuse innovations (F_t / sigma^2 >= 10^4) from the likelihood
airline_ll <- function(sys, y = as.numeric(y_ts)) {
  kf <- kfilter(y, sys); ok <- which(!is.na(kf$v))
  ok <- ok[kf$F[ok] / sys$s2 < 1e4]
  list(ll = -0.5 * sum(log(2 * pi) + log(kf$F[ok]) + kf$v[ok]^2 / kf$F[ok]), n = length(ok))
}

section: 5.3 Profile likelihoods: how well do the data pin down the variances?
text:
5.3 Profile likelihoods: how well do the data pin down the variances?
The individual variances control the filter’s behaviour, so it matters how precisely they are estimated. For the selected model I compute the profile log likelihood of each variance: fix it on a grid and maximise over the other two. A 95% confidence interval is the set of values whose profile is within \(\chi^2_{1, 0.95}/2 = 1.92\) of the maximum, which, unlike a Wald interval, works on the boundary.


Code
nm_sel <- param_names(sel$trend, sel$ar)
profile_par <- function(which_par, grid) {
  free <- setdiff(seq_along(nm_sel), which_par)
  start <- sel$theta[free]
  sapply(grid, function(val) {
    f <- function(th) { full <- numeric(length(nm_sel)); full[free] <- th
                        full[which_par] <- log(val); ssm_negll(full, y_tour, sel$trend, sel$ar) }
    o <- optim(start, f, method = "Nelder-Mead", control = list(maxit = 2000))
    start <<- o$par
    -o$value
  })
}
grids <- list(Irregular = exp(seq(log(1e-8),  log(4e-4), length.out = 30)),
              Level     = exp(seq(log(1e-4),  log(1.5e-3), length.out = 30)),
              Seasonal  = exp(seq(log(2e-5),  log(4e-4), length.out = 30)))
par_index <- c(Irregular = which(nm_sel == "eps"), Level = which(nm_sel == "level"),
               Seasonal = which(nm_sel == "seas"))
prof <- bind_rows(lapply(names(grids), function(nm)
  tibble(par = nm, value = grids[[nm]], pll = profile_par(par_index[[nm]], grids[[nm]]))))




Code
prof_rel <- prof |> mutate(rel = pll - sel$loglik)
ggplot(prof_rel, aes(value, rel)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -qchisq(0.95, 1) / 2, linetype = "dashed", colour = "firebrick") +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue4") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_scientific()) +
  facet_wrap(vars(par), scales = "free_x") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-8, 0.5)) +
  labs(x = "Variance (log scale)", y = "Profile log likelihood")

prof_ci <- prof_rel |>
  group_by(par) |>
  summarise(lo = min(value[rel >= -1.92]), hi = max(value[rel >= -1.92]),
            lo_edge = lo == min(value), hi_edge = hi == max(value), .groups = "drop")
pci <- function(p, col) prof_ci[[col]][prof_ci$par == p]








Figure 2: Profile log likelihoods of the three variances of the selected model, relative to the maximum. Values above the dashed line (−1.92) form the 95% profile confidence interval. Horizontal axes on the log scale.





The three variances behave very differently (Figure 2):

Level variance: well determined. Its 95% profile interval runs from 2.8e-04 to 7.1e-04, so the monthly standard deviation of underlying demand is between 1.7% and 2.7%. The data are informative about how fast demand moves.
Seasonal variance: moderately determined, between 2.0e-05 and 1.8e-04, so the seasonal pattern certainly changes, but the rate is known only to within a factor of about 9.
Irregular variance: on the boundary. The profile is flat from zero up to about 1.9e-04 and then falls away. The data cannot distinguish “no month-specific noise” from “a little”, but they rule out a large irregular component. This is why the estimate is essentially zero, and why a Wald interval based on the curvature at the maximum would be meaningless here.

For the filter, the flat irregular profile means that the share of each surprise treated as noise rather than signal is uncertain at the low end, but small in any case.

Figure 5: Standard deviation of the filter’s estimate of underlying demand (the level of log nights sold, so roughly a percentage), given the data up to the previous month, from February 2016 once the diffuse start has been absorbed. It settles to a steady state, grows through the COVID gap and collapses again after the restart.





With a diffuse prior the filter starts out knowing nothing (a standard deviation of \(\sqrt{10^7}\) on the log scale); after 13 months it has seen each calendar month once and the uncertainty about the level has collapsed to 3.1%. By 2016 it reaches a steady state in which the standard deviation of the level estimate is about 2.6%: the information gained each month just balances the new level shock. During the 25 missing months nothing is learned and the variance grows linearly (each month adds \(\sigma^2_\xi\), plus the seasonal uncertainty), so by March 2022 the filter’s uncertainty about the level has risen to 10.9%, 4.3 times its pre-COVID value.

  covid_rect(log_y = TRUE) +

Figure 6: One-step-ahead predictions from the filter (blue, with 95% interval) and observed log nights sold (black), 2019 to 2023. Inside the gap the blue line is the filter’s prediction carried forward from February 2020; the first observed month after the gap is far below it.





On the eve of the restart the filter predicted 2,137 thousand nights for April 2022 (95% interval 1,716 to 2,661); 1,466 thousand were sold, 31% below the prediction (Figure 6). The interval is wide because of the gap, and still did not cover the outcome: from the model’s point of view, the post-COVID reset was a level shock larger than any it had seen.
What happens next shows the gain at work. Because the uncertainty about the level was large, the gain in April 2022 gave 95% of the surprise to the level (against 66% in the steady state), so the filter moved its view of demand down almost all the way in a single month. Within a few months the gain and the level uncertainty were back to their pre-COVID steady state (Figure 5) and the one-step predictions were tracking the data again (Figure 6). The filter needed no information about when or how COVID ended; the missing-data recursion and the gain did all the work.

section: 6.3 The steady-state gain is exponential smoothing
text:
6.3 The steady-state gain is exponential smoothing


Code
pre_df <- train |> filter(Month < covid_start)
fit_pre <- fit_structural(log(pre_df$nights), sel$trend, sel$ar)
K_pre   <- fit_pre$kf$K[nrow(pre_df), ]

ets_pre <- pre_df |> model(ETS(log(nights) ~ error("A") + trend("N") + season("A")))
ets_par <- tidy(ets_pre) |> select(term, estimate) |> deframe()


Once the gain has settled to a constant \(\bar K\), the filter is \(a_{t+1} = T a_t + \bar K v_t\): a fixed share of each surprise goes to the level and a fixed share to the seasonal effect. That is exactly the error-correction form of additive Holt–Winters, ETS(A,N,A), with \(\alpha\) the level share and \(\gamma\) (roughly) the seasonal share. For the selected model the steady-state gain gives 66% of each surprise to the level and 34% to that calendar month’s seasonal effect, adding to 100% because there is no irregular component to absorb any of it.
To compare like with like I fit both models to the pre-COVID months only (ETS cannot handle the gap). The state space model’s steady-state gain is 0.41 for the level and 0.57 for the seasonal effect; ETS(A,N,A) estimates \(\alpha\) = 0.24 and \(\gamma\) = 0.76. The split between level and seasonal differs, but both add to about one: both methods conclude that a surprise in accommodation demand is almost never a one-off. The two estimators differ because ETS estimates the smoothing parameters directly by least squares on one-step errors with the initial states as free parameters, while the state space model derives them from the variances, with a diffuse start. This is the link between Projects 3 and 4: the smoothing parameters of exponential smoothing are a steady-state Kalman gain, determined by the signal-to-noise ratios.

  filter(Month >= yearmonth("2019 Jan"), Month <= yearmonth("2022 Dec")) |>
  mutate(in_gap = period == "COVID window",
         cf = if_else(in_gap, exp(signal + se^2 / 2), NA_real_),
         lo = if_else(in_gap, exp(signal - 1.96 * se), NA_real_),
         hi = if_else(in_gap, exp(signal + 1.96 * se), NA_real_),

  ggplot(aes(as.Date(Month))) +

  geom_line(aes(y = ff), colour = "darkorange", linetype = "dashed", na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_line(aes(y = exp(observed)), colour = "black") +

  labs(x = NULL, y = "Nights sold (thousands)")








Figure 9: Observed nights sold (black) during the COVID window, against two estimates of demand without COVID-19: the smoother (blue, with 95% interval), which uses the data on both sides of the gap, and the filter’s forecast made in February 2020 (orange dashed), which uses only the data before it.





The smoothed level (Figure 8) falls gently before 2020 and is lower after the gap than before it; inside the gap the smoother bridges the two. The seasonal effect hardly changes over the decade, consistent with the near-zero seasonal smoothing in Project 3. Because the COVID months were not used to estimate anything, the smoothed signal in the window is a model-based estimate of what demand would have been without the pandemic (Figure 9). Comparing it with what was actually sold, the model estimates that about 22.4 million stay unit nights were lost between March 2020 and March 2022 (95% band 18.2 to 27.0 million), or 48% of the demand expected over those 25 months.
Filtering and smoothing give two different counterfactuals. The filter’s forecast from February 2020 asks “what did we expect before the pandemic?” and puts the loss at 31.0 million nights (95% band 23.1 to 39.9 million). The smoother asks “given where demand ended up, what path is most likely?”, and because demand after the gap was lower than before it, its counterfactual drifts down through the window and the estimated loss is smaller. The smoother attributes part of the drop to a lasting change in demand that would, under the model, have happened anyway; the filter attributes all of it to COVID-19. Which is “right” depends on whether the post-COVID level reflects a permanent change that was under way regardless (the smoother’s reading) or a scar left by the pandemic (closer to the filter’s). The data cannot settle this, so I report the smoother’s figure as the main estimate and the filter’s as an upper reference.

Figure 10: Standardised smoothed level shocks (top) and seasonal shocks (bottom). A value outside ±2 (dashed) suggests a break in the level, or a change in the seasonal pattern, after that month.





The disturbance smoother estimates each month’s level and seasonal shock with hindsight (as a check, the smoothed level shocks equal the month-to-month changes in the smoothed level to within 5.7e-08). Standardised, they act as \(t\)-tests for breaks (Harvey and Koopman, 1992; Durbin and Koopman, 2012, Section 2.12). The largest level shock is at 2022 Apr (2.76), the change in the level between April and May 2022: demand on restart was depressed even relative to the new post-COVID level, and the level rose again as the recovery got going, followed by 2023 Mar (2.50) and 2017 Jan (2.20). Several of the flagged months fall in March, April or the turn of the year, the months affected by the moving Easter weekend and by when school holidays start and end. Easter falls in March in some years and April in others, and the model has no way to know this, so it partly reads a moved holiday as a level or seasonal shock. The largest seasonal shock is at 2018 Apr (-2.06). With 88 months tested, about 4 values beyond ±2 are expected by chance, and there are 3 for the level and 1 for the seasonal shocks, so apart from the post-COVID reset there is no strong evidence of other structural breaks.

title: Project 4: State Space Models for South African Accommodation Demand
text:
9.1 Forecasts on the test set
The state space forecasts are produced by kforecast() on the log scale and back-transformed with the bias adjustment \(\exp(\hat\mu + \hat\sigma^2/2)\). For comparison, the seasonal naive benchmark, the Project 1 SARIMA(0,1,1)(0,1,1)12 (COVID as missing) and the best Project 3 model, damped Holt–Winters on the regression-imputed series, are refitted here with the same code as in those projects.


Code
# Project 3 imputation of the COVID window (regression on the non-COVID months)
impute_covid <- function(df) {
  n_win <- month_num(covid_end) - month_num(covid_start) + 2
  df <- df |>
    as_tibble() |>
    mutate(t = row_number(), mon = factor(month(as.Date(Month))),
           in_win = Month >= covid_start & Month <= covid_end,
           ramp = pmin(pmax((month_num(Month) - month_num(covid_start) + 1) / n_win, 0), 1),
           y_obs = if_else(in_win, NA_real_, log(nights)))
  fit <- lm(y_obs ~ t + mon + ramp, data = df)
  df |>
    mutate(nights_imp = if_else(in_win, exp(predict(fit, newdata = df)), nights)) |>
    select(Month, nights, nights_imp, period)
}

ref_forecasts <- function(d, h) {
  dB <- d |> mutate(nights = if_else(period == "COVID window", NA_real_, nights))
  dI <- impute_covid(d) |> as_tsibble(index = Month)
  summ <- function(fc) {
    dist <- fc[[fabletools::distribution_var(fc)]]
    tibble(.model = fc$.model, Month = fc$Month, mean = fc$.mean,
           lo95 = quantile(dist, 0.025), hi95 = quantile(dist, 0.975))
  }

title: Project 4: State Space Models for South African Accommodation Demand
text:
9.3 Results
Test set. The best state space model on the test set is Damped trend + AR(1) (RMSE 89.6), against 132.6 for seasonal naive, 101.6 for the Project 1 SARIMA and 72.5 for the Project 3 damped Holt–Winters model. The lowest RMSE overall belongs to Damped HW (Project 3). The trend specification decides the ranking: the BSM, whose almost fixed slope comes from the pre-COVID decline, has an RMSE of 156.2, worse than the seasonal naive benchmark, while letting the trend die out (damped trend, RMSE 94.2) or removing it (level + seasonal, RMSE 105.9) helps a great deal (Figure 12). The best model on the test set, Damped trend + AR(1), is not the one AIC selected (Level + seasonal, RMSE 105.9): the AIC differences were small, and one-step fit in the training data is a weak guide to which trend will extrapolate best. All four state space models under-forecast (positive bias): demand grew faster in 2024 to 2026 than the models’ level and trend imply. The 95% intervals of the state space models cover every test month, with a mean width of 629 thousand nights for the best model (545 for the SARIMA). With a random-walk level and no irregular noise, all the forecast uncertainty is uncertainty about where the level will drift, and it grows steadily with the horizon.
Cross-validation. Over 13 origins the best model is SARIMA (Project 1) (RMSE 83.5) and the best state space model is Level + seasonal (RMSE 92.4). For reference, the Project 3 damped Holt-Winters model has 89.5 and seasonal naive 112.2 (Table 7, Figure 13). Given that the airline SARIMA and the level + seasonal model have almost the same likelihood (Table 3), it is not surprising that their forecasts are close; the differences come from the trend and from how each model treats the start of the series.

title: Project 4: State Space Models for South African Accommodation Demand
text:
11.1 Key findings

My implementation is correct on this series. It matches the base R Kalman routines on the accommodation data with the COVID months missing (largest state difference 1.4e-07), and it reproduces the exact log likelihood of the Project 1 airline SARIMA (147.1098 against 147.1098 from arima()).
Likelihood. The Level + seasonal model has the lowest AIC, but the four structural models and the airline SARIMA are within a few log likelihood units of each other. The level variance is well determined (monthly SD of underlying demand 1.7% to 2.7%), the irregular variance sits on the boundary at zero, and April 2022 is by far the least likely month.
Filtering. Nearly every surprise in accommodation demand is treated as lasting: the steady-state gain gives 66% to the level and 34% to the seasonal pattern, matching the near-one smoothing parameters of exponential smoothing. Through the gap the filter’s uncertainty about demand grew 4.3-fold; on restart demand was 31% below the filter’s prediction, and the filter re-learned the level within a few months without being told anything about COVID.
Smoothing. About 22.4 million stay unit nights (48% of expected demand) were lost between March 2020 and March 2022, against 31.0 million if the February 2020 forecast is used as the counterfactual. Across the four models the estimate varies by 0.4 million nights. In simulations from the fitted model the smoothed counterfactual is within about 6% of the truth in 90% of cases.
Prediction. On the test set the best state space model is Damped trend + AR(1) (RMSE 89.6, against 101.6 for the SARIMA and 72.5 for damped Holt–Winters), and the BSM with its fixed slope is the worst (RMSE 156.2).

title: Project 4: State Space Models for South African Accommodation Demand
text:
11.2 Issues and limitations

The counterfactual depends on the model. Inside the gap the smoother interpolates with a random-walk level, so the no-COVID path is close to a straight line between the pre- and post-COVID levels. The filter-versus-smoother comparison shows that the estimate of demand lost hinges on whether the lower post-COVID level is treated as something that would have happened anyway.
One set of variances for the whole decade. The innovations are more spread out after COVID than before, so the post-COVID period may need larger variances; the restart month alone has a large influence on the level variance.
Moving holidays. Easter and school holidays move between March and April, and the model reads this as level or seasonal shocks.
Approximate diffuse initialisation and boundary estimates. Using \(\kappa = 10^7\) and dropping 13 innovations uses up more than a year of data, and with the irregular variance on the boundary, AIC and likelihood ratio comparisons behave non-standardly.
Intervals ignore parameter uncertainty. The smoothing and forecast intervals treat the variances as known; the simulation study shows how much this matters for the total lost demand.
Same test window throughout. All projects use one test window and a short cross-validation period, both in the post-COVID recovery, which favours models that do not extrapolate the pre-2020 decline.

title: Project 4: State Space Models for South African Accommodation Demand
text:
11.3 What I would do differently
I would implement the exact diffuse Kalman filter, add the Project 3 intervention terms and an Easter regressor as regression effects inside the state space model (so the COVID months could be used rather than skipped and the moving holiday would no longer be read as a shock), and let the variances differ before and after COVID. A Bayesian treatment of the variances, with priors that keep the irregular variance off the boundary, would carry the parameter uncertainty into the lost-demand estimate, and a simulation smoother would give a proper interval for the total demand lost.

title: Project 2: Volatility of the South African Rand with ARCH and GARCH Models
text:
NoteExecutive summary



Title: Volatility of the South African rand with ARCH and GARCH models
Section and topic: Section 1. Conditional variance models: stylised facts of returns, testing for ARCH effects, ARCH, GARCH and asymmetric GARCH models, volatility forecasting.
Type of project: Implementation (own maximum likelihood code for GARCH(1,1), checked against rugarch and by a small simulation study) and model comparison on real-world data. The Value-at-Risk backtest is an idea not covered in the lectures.
Question: Do daily USD/ZAR exchange rate returns show volatility clustering, and which conditional variance model gives the most reliable one-day-ahead risk forecasts?
Data: Real-world, publicly available data: the South African rand to US dollar spot exchange rate (FRED series DEXSFUS, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System), daily, January 2010 to September 2026. Full source details are in Section 2.1.
Methods: Exploratory analysis of the stylised facts; Ljung and Box and ARCH LM tests; the Box and Jenkins loop applied to the mean and the variance equation; ARCH(1), GARCH(1,1) with normal and Student t errors, and GJR-GARCH(1,1) with Student t errors; my own implementation of the GARCH(1,1) likelihood; a rolling out-of-sample evaluation of 1000 one-day-ahead forecasts, scored by Value-at-Risk backtests (Kupiec and Christoffersen tests), quantile loss and QLIKE, against historical simulation and constant variance benchmarks.
Key findings: The returns show all the stylised facts: almost no autocorrelation in the returns themselves, strong autocorrelation in squared returns, and fat tails. ARCH(1) fails the residual diagnostics, while the GARCH(1,1) models capture the clustering with a very persistent variance. Student t errors fit better than normal errors, and depreciation shocks raise volatility more than appreciation shocks. Out of sample, the GJR-GARCH(1,1) t model gives the best forecasts by quantile loss and QLIKE, but all the GARCH models are too conservative in the lower tail because they assume a symmetric distribution while the returns are positively skewed; historical simulation has the best coverage. Details are in Section 9.1.
What I would do differently: Use a longer test period so that the 1% VaR tests have more power, and add a skewed Student t distribution so that the GARCH VaR can capture the asymmetry between rand depreciation and appreciation.
Detailed analysis: the sections below.

The code downloads the series the first time the document is rendered and saves it as usdzar_fred.csv. If the download fails (for example without an internet connection), download the CSV manually from the FRED page above and save it in the same folder as this file under that name.

                     "&cosd=", start_date, "&coed=", end_date)
  download.file(fred_url, data_file, mode = "wb")

fx_raw <- read.csv(data_file, na.strings = c(".", ""))
names(fx_raw) <- c("date", "rate")

fx <- fx_raw |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(date), rate = as.numeric(rate)) |>
  filter(!is.na(rate), date >= start_date, date <= end_date) |>
  arrange(date) |>
  mutate(r = 100 * (log(rate) - lag(log(rate)))) |>
  filter(!is.na(r)) |>
  mutate(day = row_number())

# tsibble indexed by trading day (the calendar dates are irregular
# because of weekends and US public holidays)
fx_ts <- fx |> as_tsibble(index = day)

r <- fx$r
n <- length(r)


Days on which FRED records no rate (US public holidays) are dropped, so returns are measured from one trading day to the next. The return is defined as
\[
r_t = 100 \times (\log P_t - \log P_{t-1}),
\]
where \(P_t\) is the number of rand per US dollar. A positive return means the rand weakened against the dollar. The analysis uses 4,188 daily returns from 5 January 2010 to 30 September 2026.
I work with log returns rather than plain differences of the rate, \(P_t - P_{t-1}\), for three reasons. First, log returns are scale-free: the rand moved from about R7.31 to R16.42 per dollar over the sample, so a 10-cent move is a 1.4% change at the start but only 0.6% at the end, and plain differences would treat these as the same shock. Second, because the size of rand moves grows with the level of the rate, plain differences show a variance that rises over time because of the trend in the level rather than volatility clustering (Figure 1), which would contaminate the variance equation. Third, multiplied by 100, a log return is approximately the percentage change, and log returns add across days, so a multi-day return is the sum of the daily ones.

p2 <- fx_ts |> ACF(r^2, lag_max = 50) |> autoplot() + labs(title = "Squared returns")

Figure 4: ACF of returns, squared returns and absolute returns, up to 50 trading days.





Figure 4 is the key plot of the project. The returns themselves have almost no autocorrelation: the largest absolute autocorrelation in the first 20 lags is only 0.042. The squared and absolute returns, in contrast, have positive autocorrelations that are significant at nearly every lag shown and decay very slowly. This is the signature of volatility clustering: the direction of tomorrow’s move is close to unpredictable, but its size depends strongly on recent sizes. The Ljung and Box test on 20 lags gives Q = 31.6 (p 0.048) for the returns and Q = 417.2 (p < 0.001) for the squared returns. The test on the returns is only just significant at the 5% level. With more than 4,000 observations even autocorrelations of about 0.04 can be detected, and correlations that small are of no practical use for forecasting the direction of the rand. After standardising by the GARCH volatility no autocorrelation remains (Table 5), so the mean equation is kept as a constant.

title: Project 2: Volatility of the South African Rand with ARCH and GARCH Models
text:
5.1 The modelling procedure for returns
The project follows the seven-step ARIMA modelling procedure (the Box and Jenkins workflow) from the lectures, as in Project 1, applied to both equations of the model:

Plot the data: done in the exploratory analysis.
Transform if needed: the rate is modelled on the log scale, so that changes are proportional to the level (Figure 1).
Difference until approximately stationary: log returns are the first difference of the log exchange rate. The returns fluctuate around a constant mean, so no further differencing is needed.
Identify candidate orders from the ACF: for the mean equation the ACF of the returns is close to zero at all lags, so a constant mean, ARMA(0,0), is used. For the variance equation the slowly decaying ACF of squared returns suggests that a low order ARCH model will not be enough and that GARCH(1,1) is the natural candidate, since it is an ARCH(\(\infty\)) model with geometrically decaying weights.
Estimate by maximum likelihood: with rugarch, and with my own code for GARCH(1,1) (Section 6).
Check the residuals against the white noise standard: the standardised residuals \(\hat z_t = \hat\varepsilon_t / \hat\sigma_t\) should show no autocorrelation (mean equation adequate) and their squares should show no autocorrelation (variance equation adequate). If a model fails, return to step 4.
Forecast: only with models that pass step 6.

Finally, a model that survives the procedure must still beat the benchmarks out of sample (Section 7).

title: Project 2: Volatility of the South African Rand with ARCH and GARCH Models
text:
5.2 Candidate models
All models have a constant mean, \(r_t = \mu + \varepsilon_t\) with \(\varepsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t\), and differ in the variance equation and in the distribution of \(z_t\):



Table 2: The four candidate models.










Model

ARCH(1)
\(\sigma_t^2 = \omega + \alpha \varepsilon_{t-1}^2\)

Normal

as above

GJR-GARCH(1,1) t
\(\sigma_t^2 = \omega + (\alpha + \gamma I_{t-1}) \varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta \sigma_{t-1}^2\), with \(I_{t-1} = 1\) if \(\varepsilon_{t-1} < 0\)
Standardised Student t






The GJR model allows good and bad news to affect volatility differently. For a share price the usual finding is that falls (negative returns) raise volatility more than rises. For USD/ZAR the interpretation is reversed: a negative return is a strengthening of the rand, so \(\gamma > 0\) would mean that rand appreciation raises volatility more, and \(\gamma < 0\) that rand depreciation raises volatility more.

Interpreting the GARCH(1,1) t fit. The ARCH coefficient \(\hat\alpha\) = 0.045 measures how strongly volatility reacts to yesterday’s shock, and \(\hat\beta\) = 0.942 measures how much of yesterday’s volatility carries over. Their sum, the persistence, is 0.9874, very close to 1. A volatility shock therefore dies out slowly, with a half-life of about 55 trading days. 6.1 A small simulation check
Agreement with a package shows that two implementations agree, not that either is right. As a second check, I simulated 100 series of the same length as the data from a GARCH(1,1) with known parameters (set equal to the rugarch estimates) and refitted each one with my code.

sim_garch11 <- function(n, mu, omega, alpha, beta, burn = 500) {
  N <- n + burn
  z <- rnorm(N); e <- s2 <- numeric(N)
  s2[1] <- omega / (1 - alpha - beta)
  e[1]  <- sqrt(s2[1]) * z[1]
  for (t in 2:N) {
    s2[t] <- omega + alpha * e[t - 1]^2 + beta * s2[t - 1]
    e[t]  <- sqrt(s2[t]) * z[t]
  }
  mu + e[(burn + 1):N]
}

The first time I ran this check, the results did not match the theory: in almost half of the replications my code returned \(\hat\alpha = 0\) and \(\hat\beta = 1\), a constant variance model, even though every series was simulated with clear GARCH effects. The problem was the optimiser, not the likelihood. 7.1 Design
In-sample fit does not answer the research question, which is about forecasts. The last 1000 trading days (from 30 September 2022 to 30 September 2026) are used as a test period. For each day in the test period, every model produces a one-day-ahead forecast of the mean and standard deviation using only data up to the previous day. The GARCH models are re-estimated every 25 trading days on an expanding window, which keeps the evaluation free of temporal leakage.
From each forecast distribution I compute the VaR at four levels: the 1% and 5% quantiles (losses for someone holding dollars when the rand strengthens) and the 95% and 99% quantiles (losses for someone who needs dollars, such as an importer, when the rand weakens). For Student t models,
\[
\text{VaR}_{p,t} = \hat\mu_{t|t-1} + \hat\sigma_{t|t-1} \, t_{\nu}^{-1}(p) \sqrt{(\nu - 2)/\nu},
\]
where the last factor rescales the t distribution to unit variance.
Two benchmarks without a GARCH variance are included, in the spirit of the benchmark methods in the notes:

Historical simulation (HS): the VaR is the empirical quantile of the previous 250 returns.
Rolling normal: a normal distribution with the mean and variance of the previous 250 returns.

The ARCH(1) model failed the residual diagnostics, so following step 7 it is not part of the forecast comparison.

7.2 Backtest tests
For each model and level, a hit is a day on which the realised return falls beyond the VaR (below it for the 1% and 5% levels, above it for the 95% and 99% levels). Under a correct model the hits are independent Bernoulli(\(p^*\)) variables, where \(p^* = p\) for the lower tail and \(p^* = 1 - p\) for the upper tail. I implemented two standard likelihood ratio tests.

Kupiec unconditional coverage test: is the hit rate equal to \(p^*\)? With \(x\) hits in \(T\) days and \(\hat\pi = x / T\), \(LR_{uc} = -2 \left[ (T - x)\log(1 - p^*) + x \log p^* - (T - x)\log(1 - \hat\pi) - x \log \hat\pi \right] \sim \chi^2_1 .\)
Christoffersen conditional coverage test: adds a test of independence, comparing a first-order Markov chain for the hits with an independent sequence, so that clustered hits are detected. \(LR_{cc} = LR_{uc} + LR_{ind} \sim \chi^2_2\).



Code
kupiec_test <- function(hits, p) {
  n <- length(hits); x <- sum(hits); phat <- x / n
  ll0 <- (n - x) * log(1 - p) + x * log(p)
  ll1 <- if (x == 0 || x == n) 0 else (n - x) * log(1 - phat) + x * log(phat)
  lr  <- -2 * (ll0 - ll1)
  c(hits = x, expected = n * p, LR_uc = lr, p_uc = pchisq(lr, 1, lower.tail = FALSE))
}

christoffersen_test <- function(hits, p) {
  h0 <- hits[-length(hits)]; h1 <- hits[-1]
  n00 <- sum(h0 == 0 & h1 == 0); n01 <- sum(h0 == 0 & h1 == 1)
  n10 <- sum(h0 == 1 & h1 == 0); n11 <- sum(h0 == 1 & h1 == 1)
  pi01 <- n01 / (n00 + n01)
  pi11 <- if ((n10 + n11) > 0) n11 / (n10 + n11) else 0
  pi1  <- (n01 + n11) / (n00 + n01 + n10 + n11)
  xlogy <- function(x, y) ifelse(x == 0, 0, x * log(y))
  ll_ind <- xlogy(n00, 1 - pi01) + xlogy(n01, pi01) +
            xlogy(n10, 1 - pi11) + xlogy(n11, pi11)
  ll_dep <- xlogy(n00 + n10, 1 - pi1) + xlogy(n01 + n11, pi1)
  lr_ind <- -2 * (ll_dep - ll_ind)
  lr_cc  <- kupiec_test(hits, p)[["LR_uc"]] + lr_ind
  c(p_ind = pchisq(lr_ind, 1, lower.tail = FALSE),
    p_cc  = pchisq(lr_cc, 2, lower.tail = FALSE))
}

                                 "Historical simulation" = "steelblue")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Return (%)", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")








Figure 7: Test period returns with the 1% and 99% one-day VaR from the GARCH(1,1) t model (red) and historical simulation (blue). Points mark returns beyond the GARCH 1% or 99% VaR.





Coverage. Out of the four levels, the number of rejections (Kupiec or Christoffersen test at 5%) is 1 for GARCH(1,1) normal, 3 for GARCH(1,1) t, 2 for GJR-GARCH(1,1) t, 0 for historical simulation and 2 for the rolling normal benchmark. On this count the crudest method, historical simulation, is the best calibrated.
The pattern behind the GARCH rejections is more informative than the counts. They are almost all in the lower tail, and they come from too few hits rather than too many: at the 5% level all three GARCH models are exceeded only 29 times against 50 expected. In the upper tail, where the rand weakens, the GARCH models are close to the expected numbers at both levels. So the GARCH VaR is too conservative on days when the rand strengthens and about right on days when it weakens. The reason is that every model here uses a symmetric distribution for \(z_t\), while the returns are positively skewed: the skewness is 0.20 over the test period and 0.22 over the full sample, so large weakening moves are more common than strengthening moves of the same size. A symmetric distribution has to share its tail probability equally between the two sides, which overstates the lower tail. Historical simulation uses the empirical quantiles directly, so it picks up the skewness automatically.
Normal or t out of sample. At the 1% level, where a correct model should be exceeded about 10 times, the GARCH(1,1) normal model is exceeded 7 times in the lower tail and 10 times in the upper tail, against 4 and 9 for the GARCH(1,1) t model. Neither model is exceeded too often. The heavier tails of the t distribution push its 1% VaR further out, which in the already over-covered lower tail makes it more conservative (rejected by the Kupiec test, p 0.030). The clear in-sample advantage of t errors therefore does not show up as better coverage in this test period, although it does show up in the loss functions below.
Clustering of exceedances. The benchmarks react slowly to a change in volatility, because a window of 250 days gives a return from a year ago the same weight as yesterday’s. Their VaR therefore moves in slow steps (Figure 7), staying too wide for months after volatility falls and too narrow after it jumps. In this test period the cost of that slowness was small. The test period was calmer than the training period (daily standard deviation 0.83% against 0.97%), with no volatility jump on the scale of 2016 or 2020, and the Christoffersen test does not reject historical simulation at any level. The rolling normal benchmark is rejected at two levels: at 5%, like the GARCH models, it has too few hits, and at 99% its normal tails are too thin (18 hits against 10 expected). The GARCH(1,1) t model is rejected by the Christoffersen test at the 95% level (p 0.034) even though its hit count is almost exactly right, so some of its upper-tail hits came in pairs. The GARCH VaR bands widen and narrow within days, which is the behaviour that matters when volatility does change quickly.
Ranking. Averaged over the four levels, the lowest quantile loss is achieved by the GJR-GARCH(1,1) t model, and the lowest QLIKE by the GJR-GARCH(1,1) t model. Both are proper scoring rules, so they reward forecasts that are close to the truth across the whole period, not just a correct hit count. The differences between the three GARCH models are small and were not tested formally, so the ranking among them is indicative; the gap between the GARCH models and the rolling normal benchmark on QLIKE is much larger.
Answer to the research question. The returns clearly show volatility clustering, and no single model wins on every criterion. The GJR-GARCH(1,1) t model gives the best one-day-ahead risk forecasts overall: it has the lowest quantile loss and QLIKE, it captures the asymmetry between depreciation and appreciation, and its VaR is well calibrated in the upper tail, which is the tail that matters to someone exposed to a weaker rand. Its weakness is the lower tail, where its symmetric error distribution makes the VaR too conservative, and there the distribution-free historical simulation is better calibrated. A GARCH model with a skewed error distribution would be the natural way to combine the strengths of both.

title: Project 2: Volatility of the South African Rand with ARCH and GARCH Models
text:
9.1 Key findings

The rand shows all the stylised facts of financial returns: almost no autocorrelation in returns, strong and slowly decaying autocorrelation in squared returns, and fat tails (excess kurtosis 1.9). The ARCH LM test confirms a time-varying variance (p < 0.001).
The Box and Jenkins loop rejected ARCH(1) because ARCH structure remained in its standardised residuals, and led to GARCH(1,1).
Volatility is highly persistent: \(\hat\alpha + \hat\beta\) = 0.9874, a half-life of about 55 trading days.
Student t errors are clearly better than normal errors (\(\hat\nu\) = 11.0), so even after removing volatility clustering, extreme days are more common than a normal distribution implies.
Asymmetry: \(\hat\gamma\) = -0.051 (p < 0.001). There is significant asymmetry in how depreciation and appreciation shocks affect volatility.
Out of sample, the preferred model by quantile loss is GJR-GARCH(1,1) t and by QLIKE GJR-GARCH(1,1) t. But all the GARCH models are too conservative in the lower tail (29 hits at 5% against 50 expected), because they assume a symmetric distribution while the returns are positively skewed. Historical simulation is the only method with no rejected VaR tests. In the upper tail, which matters to someone exposed to a weaker rand, the GARCH hit counts are close to the expected numbers, and the GJR-GARCH(1,1) t model passes both tests at both upper levels.
The simulation check found an optimiser problem in my own GARCH code: R’s BFGS stopped at the degenerate corner \(\alpha = 0\), \(\beta = 1\) in almost half of the replications until the objective was rescaled.

title: Project 2: Volatility of the South African Rand with ARCH and GARCH Models
text:
9.2 Issues and limitations

Power of the tests. With 1000 test days, a correct 1% VaR is expected to be exceeded only 10 times, so the Kupiec test has little power to separate a 1% model from, say, a 1.5% model. A model that “passes” is not proven correct.
Tests with a large sample. The residual tests in-sample use more than 4000 observations, so even very small departures from white noise can be significant. I combined the formal tests with the plots and the out-of-sample results rather than relying on p-values alone.
Very high persistence. A persistence close to 1 can be a sign of structural breaks in the level of volatility (for example a calmer period after 2020) rather than true long memory, as discussed in the notes. A model with a regime change in volatility, such as a hidden Markov model, would be a natural alternative.
Data choices. FRED noon rates in New York miss moves that happen during South African trading hours after the New York fix, and dropping US holidays makes some returns cover two days. Neither should affect the conclusions much, but a Johannesburg close series would be a useful check.
Refitting every 25 days rather than daily saves time but means the parameters lag slightly behind; the volatility itself is still updated every day.
Symmetric error distributions. All the models assume that, given the volatility, a strengthening and a weakening of the same size are equally likely. The backtest shows that this is the main weakness of the GARCH VaR for the rand.
Size of the loss differences. The QLIKE and quantile loss differences between the three GARCH models are small and were not tested formally (for example with a Diebold and Mariano test).
VaR is only one risk measure. It says nothing about how large losses are once the VaR is exceeded. Expected shortfall would be the natural extension.

title: Project 2: Volatility of the South African Rand with ARCH and GARCH Models
text:
9.3 What I would do differently
I would add a skewed Student t distribution (available in rugarch) so that the GARCH VaR can reflect the positive skewness found in the backtest, use a longer test period so that the 1% tests have more power, and add expected shortfall to the backtest. A further comparison would be a hidden Markov model that lets volatility switch between a small number of regimes, using the same returns and the same backtest.

title: Project 2: Volatility of the South African Rand with ARCH and GARCH Models
text:
9.4 Reflection and model development
Going into this project, I knew that ARCH and GARCH models are built to model volatility directly. They don’t try to predict which way a series moves; they predict how much it moves. I felt that currencies were the place to test that, because exchange rates are famously volatile and close to unpredictable in direction. The rand in particular has been going through a very interesting period. It weakened to R19.82 per dollar in April 2025, its weakest level in my sample, then strengthened steadily to around R15.80 by January 2026. Over the same two years the conflict involving Iran escalated, and when war broke out between the United States and Iran at the end of February 2026, the rand went from months of calm to moving by 2 to 3% in a day. That is exactly the kind of behaviour GARCH models are designed for, and because these events fall inside my test period, I could see how the models handled a real shock rather than only a historical one. It also connected back to Project 1, where my first idea had been to use financial data until its volatility made it a poor fit for ARIMA models. This project let me return to that idea with the right tools, but taking it in a more macroeconomic direction than a purely financial one.
The model was not chosen in one step; each decision came from something I saw in the data. The first was to work with log returns rather than the exchange rate itself. The rate trends from about R7 to almost R20 over the sample, so the level is not stationary, and plain daily changes in rand grow as the level rises. Log returns fix both problems, following the same transform-then-difference logic as Project 1. Next I looked at the ACF, expecting it to tell me which ARMA terms to use. However, the ACF of the returns was flat, so there was nothing for AR or MA terms to pick up and the mean equation became just a constant. Since the returns themselves showed no structure, I followed the approach in our class notes and looked at the squared returns, which act as a measure of the size of each day’s shock. That is where the real signal appeared: the autocorrelations were positive and still significant after 50 trading days. The direction of tomorrow’s move cannot be predicted, but its size can, and the ARCH LM test confirmed that the variance is not constant.
From there I built up the variance model step by step. I started with the simplest option, ARCH(1), but it failed the residual checks because ARCH structure was still left over. The slowly decaying ACF of the squared returns showed why: an ARCH model would need dozens of lags to capture that long memory, while GARCH(1,1) achieves it with one extra parameter, because the lagged variance carries all earlier shocks forward. The residuals still showed heavy tails, so I replaced the normal distribution with a Student t. And because the most violent episodes in the data, in 2015, 2020 and 2026, were all times when the rand weakened, I added the GJR term so that depreciation and appreciation could affect volatility differently. It turned out to be significant: shocks that weaken the rand raise volatility far more than shocks that strengthen it. Since my question was about forecasting risk, I did not stop at in-sample fit, and instead judged the models in a rolling one-day-ahead Value-at-Risk backtest against two simple benchmarks.
The project went through several phases, each driven by a decision about what would make the analysis more reliable or easier to follow. My early drafts focused on getting the full analysis working as a stand-alone report: the models, my own GARCH code, the simulation check and the backtest. As the analysis settled, my focus shifted from getting results to justifying them, starting with an explicit argument for using log returns, since that was the first modelling decision and everything else built on it. The biggest change came when I stepped back and critically reviewed the whole project, which led to the coding and modelling improvements that made the final version far more reliable.
The most important of these was a problem I almost missed. My GARCH code matched rugarch exactly on the real data, so I assumed it was correct, but the simulation check showed otherwise: in almost half of the simulated series my code returned a constant-variance model, even though every series had clear GARCH effects. I really struggled to identify where the issue was and used an LLM to help investigate it. The cause turned out to be the optimiser. With such a large log likelihood, R’s BFGS took a first step so big that it landed in a flat region and stopped. Rescaling the objective fixed it, and the estimates then sat right on the true values. Getting the fix to show up taught me a second lesson: because the simulation was cached, R would have kept showing the old results until I forced that chunk to run again. Both problems showed me that code can look right without being right, and that matching a package only shows that two programs agree on one dataset. The simulation, where I knew the true answer, was what exposed the problem.
The backtest taught me to look at the pattern behind a result rather than just the headline. Historical simulation, the simplest method, was the only one with no rejected tests, and every GARCH rejection came from too few hits in the lower tail. The explanation was that the rand’s returns are positively skewed, but all my models assume a symmetric distribution, so they overstate the risk of large strengthening moves. That ended up being one of the most interesting findings of the project. It also showed me that different evaluation measures answer different questions: the loss functions said GJR-GARCH with t errors gave the best forecasts overall, while the coverage tests said historical simulation was better calibrated, and both were true. Finally, tidying up outdated references and aligning the procedure with Project 1 made the whole report more consistent and easier to trust.
Going forward, the natural next step is a GARCH model with a skewed Student t distribution, which would keep GARCH’s ability to react to shocks within days while fixing the lower tail. I would also like to look more closely at the weeks of the US–Iran war inside the test period, to see how each model coped while the shock was happening, and to add expected shortfall, since VaR says nothing about how large losses are on the days it is exceeded.
