title: Week 10
text:
Session or topic covered: Kalman Filter 
This week was all about the Kalman filter. I worked through the lecture slides and the second half of the state space chapter, and the parts I found hardest were the three updating equations, why the intervals are called prediction intervals, and the difference between filtering and smoothing.
The idea itself is simple once you see it. The Kalman filter estimates a hidden state over time by combining what the model predicts the state should be with what we actually observe. Neither is perfect: the prediction carries uncertainty and the observation carries noise, so the filter weighs the two by how much each can be trusted. A phone’s live location works this way. The GPS reading jumps around by a few metres, but your true position moves smoothly, so combining where you probably are (based on where you were a moment ago) with the noisy reading gives a better estimate than either alone.
What made it click for me was thinking about it in Bayesian terms. At each time step, the prediction from the previous step is the prior, the new observation gives the likelihood, and combining them gives the posterior, which then becomes the prior for the next step:
\[
\pi(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t}) \propto \pi(y_t \mid \theta_t)\, \pi(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t-1}).
\]
Because everything is normal, the posterior stays normal, so the filter only ever has to keep track of a mean and a variance.
The equations with \(F\), \(G\), \(W\) and \(V\) felt abstract until I worked them out for the local level model,
\[
y_t = \theta_t + v_t, \quad v_t \sim N(0, V), \qquad \theta_t = \theta_{t-1} + w_t, \quad w_t \sim N(0, W),
\]
where \(F = G = 1\) and everything is a single number.
First, predict the state:
\[
a_t = m_{t-1}, \qquad R_t = C_{t-1} + W.
\]
My best guess for today’s level is yesterday’s estimate, but I’m less certain about it because the level could have moved, which is why the state noise \(W\) gets added to the variance.
Second, predict the observation:
\[
f_t = a_t, \qquad Q_t = R_t + V.
\]
The predicted observation is just the predicted state, but its variance is bigger because it includes uncertainty about the state plus the observation noise \(V\).
Third, update once \(y_t\) comes in. The forecast error and the Kalman gain are
\[
e_t = y_t - f_t, \qquad K_t = \frac{R_t}{R_t + V},
\]
and \(K_t\) always sits between 0 and 1. The update can be rewritten as
\[
m_t = a_t + K_t e_t = (1 - K_t)\, a_t + K_t\, y_t,
\]
and this was the most useful thing I worked out all week. The new estimate is just a weighted average of my prediction and the observation. If the observations are very noisy (large \(V\)), \(K_t\) is close to 0 and I mostly trust my prediction. If the state moves around a lot (large \(W\), so large \(R_t\)), \(K_t\) is close to 1 and I mostly trust the new observation. The variance update
\[
C_t = (1 - K_t)\, R_t
\]
shows that observing something always shrinks the uncertainty.
Missing values then made sense straight away. If \(y_t\) is missing there’s no new information, so \(K_t = 0\), giving \(m_t = a_t\) and \(C_t = R_t\). The posterior equals the prior and the uncertainty keeps growing through \(W\). In the Nile example with 1910 to 1915 removed, the filtered level goes flat and the bands widen over exactly those years.
The prediction interval question confused me for a while. The interval
\[
f_t \pm 1.96\sqrt{Q_t}
\]
describes where the next observation will land, so it includes both the uncertainty about the state and the observation noise. That’s what makes it a prediction interval. A confidence interval would be about the state itself and would use \(C_t\) instead.
I also kept mixing up filtering and smoothing. Filtering estimates the state at time \(t\) using only data up to \(t\), so it reacts to every new observation and jumps around. Smoothing runs backwards once all the data is in and estimates where the state was at time \(t\) using everything, including later observations, which is why the smoothed Nile level is so much less jumpy.
Finally, the likelihood fell into place. Each one-step-ahead prediction satisfies \(y_t \mid y_{1:t-1} \sim N(f_t, Q_t)\), so the likelihood is just a product of these normals:
\[
\ell(\phi) = -\frac{1}{2}\sum_{t=1}^{n} \log Q_t - \frac{1}{2}\sum_{t=1}^{n} \frac{(y_t - f_t)^2}{Q_t}.
\]
That’s what lets \(V\) and \(W\) be estimated by maximum likelihood instead of assumed known, although the surface can be flat or have several peaks, so it’s worth trying different starting values. Next I want to write the filter myself from scratch, check it against dlm on simulated data and the Nile series, and then add the smoother and likelihood so I can estimate the variances on my own.

title: Week 04
text:
Session or topic covered:Operators, Stationarity and White Noise 
This week covered operators, stationarity and white noise, and at first it felt like the most abstract week so far. When I first saw the lag operator I didn’t see the point of it, because writing \(Ly_t = y_{t-1}\) seemed like a complicated way of saying the previous value. It made more sense once I thought of an operator as a shortcut for moving around a time series. \(L\) takes you back one period and the lead operator \(F\) takes you forward one. Many real series, like GDP, inflation and exchange rates, depend on their own recent past, and operators give a clean way to describe that without writing out the value two periods ago every time.
The direction of the shift confused me. Take the series 3, 7, 4, 8, 5 observed at times 1 to 5. Applying \(L\) gives NA, 3, 7, 4, 8. At time 2 the lagged value is 3, which was observed at time 1, and at time 1 there is nothing earlier, so there is a gap. I expected a lag to move things backwards, but the subscript records where the value came from, not where it is displayed, so the series shifts to the right. The lead operator does the opposite and gives 7, 4, 8, 5, NA. I also had to be careful not to read \(L^2 y_t\) as \((y_{t-1})^2\). It means applying the lag twice, so \(L^2 y_t = y_{t-2}\). Lagging is also different from differencing: lagging only moves a value to a new time label, while \((1 - L)y_t = y_t - y_{t-1}\) creates a new series of changes.
For stationarity, what helped me was realising that the values can move around while the rules generating them stay the same. The mean and variance are constant, and the covariance between two observations depends only on how far apart they are, not on when they occur. This made it clear why a series with a trend or seasonality is not stationary, since in both cases the mean depends on when you look. I didn’t see the point of ergodicity at first, but it clicked when I realised we only ever observe one realisation of a process. Ergodicity means that averaging over time along that one long series gives the same answer as averaging across all the series the process could have produced.
Transformations were the most confusing part for me. I thought the reason for transforming a series was to make it normal, but I had mixed two ideas together. A log or Box-Cox transform is mainly there to stabilise the variance when the spread grows with the level, because it shrinks large values more than small ones. Normality is a separate question. Once I separated these, I could match each problem to its fix: a transformation for growing variance, removing a fitted trend when the trend is deterministic, differencing when it is stochastic, seasonal differencing for seasonality that doesn’t fade, and splitting the sample at a structural break. Transforming before differencing also makes sense, since stabilising the variance first often means less differencing is needed.
I didn’t understand why white noise got so much attention until I saw that it is what we want our residuals to look like. If the residuals still show a pattern, the model has missed something, and if they look like white noise, it has captured the linear structure. Weak white noise only requires the observations to be uncorrelated, while strict white noise requires them to be independent and identically distributed. The key for me was that uncorrelated does not mean independent, because correlation only measures linear relationships. For example, if \(x\) is equally likely to be \(-1\), \(0\) or \(1\) and \(y = x^2\), then \(y\) is completely determined by \(x\), yet their correlation is zero, because \(y\) rises whether \(x\) is negative or positive, so there is no straight-line pattern.
Finally, we saw how dependence can be built from white noise using \[
y_t = \tfrac{1}{3}(\varepsilon_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t + \varepsilon_{t+1}).
\] Each value is a weighted combination of three nearby shocks. The shocks are unrelated, but \(y_t\) and \(y_{t+1}\) share \(\varepsilon_t\) and \(\varepsilon_{t+1}\), so they are correlated and the result is no longer white noise. This is called filtering. I also saw why this filter is useful for smoothing but not for forecasting, because it uses \(\varepsilon_{t+1}\), a future shock we would never have when making a forecast. A forecasting model can only combine current and past shocks.

title: Week 02
text:
Stationary and Random Walks Generally I found this weeks work quite intuitive. Generally the weeks are moving quite slowly with small amounts of theory covered everything. At first when I revised this weeks content, I found the concept of growing uncertainty confusing because I assumed that as we forecast further into the future, the uncertainty would simply continue increasing in the same way for all time-series models. I initially struggled to understand why the prediction intervals for a random walk continue to widen indefinitely, while those of a stationary AR(1) model eventually level off. I now understand that the difference comes from how each process responds to shocks. In a random walk, shocks accumulate over time, meaning that the further ahead we forecast, the more uncertainty builds up. In a stationary AR(1) process, however, the effects of shocks gradually disappear and the process returns towards its long-run mean. Therefore, although uncertainty initially increases as the forecasting horizon grows, it eventually reaches a finite limit. This helped me understand that forecasting further into the future does not always mean uncertainty grows without bound; it depends on whether the underlying process is stationary or non-stationary.

At first I don’t really understand the idea of smoothing out high frequency structures and how aggregation reveals a frequency structure, these words were quite complicated and confusing and therefore after a bit of research understand exactly what this meant. Usually when I feel confused about a topic I ask AI To explain the concept not just mathematically or statistically but intuitively so that I can understand the idea in a trivial way and build it up into a deaper foundational understanindg. I now understand that the granularity is when you change the resolution so that you can see a deeper pattern as you change the granularity you’re going to notice deeper patterns when you focus on a smaller subset or deep dive into a particular segment. For example hourly temperature data may show fluctuations throughout the day while daily data only shows the average temperature the temperature doesn’t really change but we’re seeing a different level of detail as we move further in. So now I understand what the notes meant by nothing changes about the underlying process only what we see changes.
During class we discussed the difference between prediction and forecasting, which I initially found confusing. After doing some research, I now understand forecasting as a specific type of prediction. Both involve using available information to estimate an unknown quantity, but forecasting specifically focuses on estimating a future value, often by using historical time-series data and assuming that patterns observed in the past may continue into the future. Prediction is a broader concept and does not necessarily involve time or historical data.
From the initial introduction to time series I think one of the most important slides and conversations we had in class was around the goals and planning. The loop of the forecasting to goal to plan to implement and to outcome is extremely important in understanding the life cycle of the forecaster data and helps me understand how exactly to go about setting a goal and planning how we should go about organizing and managing the data which I think will be extremely helpful and impact when dealing with major projects.

title: Week 03
text:
Session or topic covered:Residuals, Train and Test Samples and Validation
I actually really enjoyed the start of this weeks material. I found the concepts generally quite standard for a statistical anlysis and I could start visualizing a bit more clearly how a project or genuine analysis could shape.
My first issues started to appear when I initially didn’t really understand the difference between residuals and forecast errors because both are essentially measuring how wrong the model is. I now understand that the key difference is what data we are measuring the error on. Residuals are the errors on data the model has already seen and used to fit itself, so they are useful for checking the model’s fit and diagnosing problems. Forecast errors are the errors on new data that the model has never seen, so they tell us how well the model actually predicts. This also helped me understand why small residuals don’t necessarily mean the model will forecast well.
One thing I found particularly interesting was the idea of temporal ordering in forecasting. I initially thought that when splitting data into training and validation sets, we could simply choose observations randomly, like we often do in other statistical or machine learning problems. However, with time series, this would allow information from the future to influence the model, which would not reflect how forecasting actually works. The rule that every training observation must come before every validation observation makes intuitive sense because, when we are forecasting the future, we can only use information that was available at that point in time. This also helped me understand temporal leakage as a model that can appear extremely accurate if it accidentally uses future information, but that accuracy is misleading because we would not have access to that information when making a real forecast.
I initially found rolling-origin evaluation quite confusing, but it helped once I thought of it as repeatedly pretending to be at different points in the past. Instead of having one fixed train/test split, we move the forecasting point forward through time, each time using only the data that would have been available at that point to predict what comes next. For example, we could use January–June to predict July, then January–July to predict August, and so on. I used an LLM to visually understand how the validation metjods could work and this immediatley helped to understand it in a bit of a different and intuitive way. We then look at all the forecast errors together. I like the intuition that we are essentially asking, if I had been making forecasts at different points in time, how well would my model have performed? This gives us a more reliable picture of forecasting accuracy than relying on just one train/test split.

title: Project 1: Forecasting South African Accommodation Demand with ARIMA and SARIMA Models
text:
NoteExecutive summary



Title: Forecasting South African accommodation demand with ARIMA and SARIMA models
Section and topic: Section 1. Benchmarks, stationarity and differencing, ARMA, ARIMA and SARIMA models, the Box and Jenkins workflow, forecast evaluation.
Type of project: Implementation and model comparison on real-world data.
Question: How much forecast accuracy is gained by moving from simple benchmark methods to ARMA, ARIMA and seasonal ARIMA models for monthly stay unit nights sold in South Africa, and how sensitive is that gain to the way the COVID-19 structural break is handled?
Data: Real-world, publicly available data from Statistics South Africa (Stats SA), Tourist Accommodation statistical release P6410, series B64100 (stay unit nights sold, total industry, thousands), monthly. Analysis window January 2015 to June 2026. Full source details are in Section 2.1.
Methods: The analysis follows the seven-step ARIMA modelling procedure from the lectures (plot, transform, difference, identify, estimate, check residuals, forecast). In the main analysis the COVID months (March 2020 to March 2022) are treated as missing, so all models are estimated from the pre- and post-COVID data only; fitting the same models with the COVID months kept is reported as a sensitivity check. The transformation and the orders of differencing are chosen from the pre-COVID data using time plots, ACF/PACF plots and unit root tests, with the Guerrero estimate of the Box–Cox parameter reported as a check. A candidate SARIMA model is identified by hand from the ACF and PACF and compared with the model chosen automatically by ARIMA(). Each candidate is checked with residual plots, Ljung–Box tests and, for the final model, its MA roots. The candidates are then compared with four benchmarks (mean, naive, seasonal naive, drift) and simpler ARMA and ARIMA models on a 24-month test set (RMSE, MAE, MAPE, MASE, interval coverage) and by expanding-window rolling-origin cross-validation over horizons of 1 to 12 months.
Target variable: This analysis focuses on stay unit nights sold. This was chosen over income level and occupancy rate because it appears to be the most consistent. Occupancy rate can change when room supply changes and income can be disrupted by inflation or other general increases. Unit nights sold tells a very clear demand picture with minimal factors affecting the quality of the variable over the years.
Key findings: See Section 9.1. In short: with the COVID months left in the data, the seasonal ARIMA models are far worse than the seasonal naive benchmark, because the collapse in April 2020 dominates the estimated variance and distorts the parameters. Treating the COVID window as missing gives a stable SARIMA(0,1,1)(0,1,1)12 “airline” model with well behaved residuals, and that model gives the most accurate forecasts on both the test set and in cross-validation.
What I would do differently: Model the shock explicitly with intervention variables (taken up in Project 3), and compare the expanding window with a sliding window that forgets the pre-COVID years.
Detailed analysis: the sections below.

Figure 1 shows three distinct regimes. Before 2020 the series moves around a fairly flat level of about 2,212 thousand nights a month (2019 average) with a strong and regular seasonal pattern. The series is clearly not stationary in mean over the full window, and the variability is much larger during the COVID window than anywhere else.

3.5 Stationarity and identification (pre-COVID data)
Identification is done on the pre-COVID data only, because the COVID collapse would dominate any ACF calculated over the full series and hide the ordinary dependence structure.

d12 <- diff(lx, lag = 12)

kpss_d12 <- unitroot_kpss(d12)

  `KPSS statistic` = c(kpss_lx["kpss_stat"], kpss_d12["kpss_stat"]),
  `KPSS p-value`   = c(kpss_lx["kpss_pvalue"], kpss_d12["kpss_pvalue"]),

The seasonal strength test suggests 1 seasonal difference for the log series, and the seasonal difference is taken. The first difference is a judgement call, because here the tests and the plots disagree. The KPSS test does not reject stationarity of the seasonally differenced series, and ndiffs suggests 0 further first differences. The KPSS p-values are interpolated from a table that only runs from 0.01 to 0.1, so a reported value of 0.1 should be read as “at least 0.1”. However, Figure 6 still shows a slowly decaying ACF over the first several lags, the classic sign of a wandering level. With only 62 pre-COVID months the tests have little power to detect a unit root. The time plot also shows that the level after COVID settled below its pre-COVID value, which a model with a fixed mean cannot represent. For these reasons one first difference is taken despite the test result. The fitted non-seasonal MA coefficient is checked later for signs of over-differencing; a value near -1 would point to over-differencing.


Code
pre_covid |>
  gg_tsdisplay(difference(log(nights), 12), plot_type = "partial", lag_max = 36)








Figure 6: Seasonally differenced log nights sold (pre-COVID) with its ACF and PACF.







Code
pre_covid |>
  gg_tsdisplay(difference(difference(log(nights), 12)), plot_type = "partial", lag_max = 36)








Figure 7: Seasonally and first differenced log nights sold (pre-COVID) with its ACF and PACF.





After both differences (Figure 7) the series looks stationary. The ACF has a clear negative spike at lag 1 (r1 = -0.39) and the PACF tails off over the first few lags, which points to a non-seasonal MA(1) term. The lag 12 autocorrelation is small (r12 = 0.11) and well inside the 95% bounds in Figure 7, so the ACF on its own does not show a clear seasonal MA signature. The isolated spike at lag 9 (and the borderline one at lag 13) has no seasonal interpretation; with 36 lags shown, one or two exceedances are expected by chance, so these are not modelled. A seasonal MA(1) term is still included, for two reasons. First, a seasonal difference usually induces negative autocorrelation at the seasonal lag, and a seasonal MA(1) is the standard term for it. Second, the short pre-COVID sample makes the lag 12 estimate imprecise. The term is kept only if its fitted coefficient is clearly non-zero, which is checked in Table 5. Following the Box and Jenkins workflow, the hand identified model is
\[
(1 - L)(1 - L^{12}) \log y_t = (1 + \theta_1 L)(1 + \Theta_1 L^{12})\,\varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t \sim \text{WN}(0, \sigma^2),
\]
the SARIMA(0,1,1)(0,1,1)12 or “airline” model. No constant is included because with d + D = 2 a constant would imply a quadratic trend in the forecasts.

title: Project 1: Forecasting South African Accommodation Demand with ARIMA and SARIMA Models
text:
4.1 The ARIMA modelling procedure
The modelling follows the seven-step ARIMA modelling procedure (the Box and Jenkins workflow) from the lectures. Each step maps to a part of this report:

Plot the data: the time plot, seasonal plots and STL decomposition in the exploratory analysis.
Transform if needed to stabilise the variance: a log transformation, chosen from the proportional seasonal swings. The Guerrero estimate is reported but not followed, for the reasons given in the exploratory analysis.
Difference until approximately stationary: one seasonal and one first difference of log nights sold, chosen from the unit root tests, the ACF and the time plot.
Identify candidate orders from the ACF and PACF: the lag 1 spike, together with the seasonal difference, points to the SARIMA(0,1,1)(0,1,1)12 model. The model chosen automatically by ARIMA() is included as an alternative candidate.
Estimate by maximum likelihood: ARIMA() in fable, in the main analysis and in the sensitivity check.
Check the residuals against the white noise standard: Ljung and Box tests, residual plots, ACF and histogram. If a model fails, return to step 4.
Forecast: only with models that pass step 6.

Finally, a model that survives the procedure must still beat the benchmarks on the test set before it earns its place. In this report, models that fail step 6 are still forecast on the test set, but only as reference points showing why the loop matters. They are not candidates for the final model.

title: Project 1: Forecasting South African Accommodation Demand with ARIMA and SARIMA Models
text:
4.2 The COVID problem
ARIMA models assume that one set of parameters describes the whole series. The COVID window breaks this in two ways. First, the April 2020 collapse produces residuals many times larger than normal, which inflates \(\hat\sigma^2\) and therefore every prediction interval. Second, the estimation tries to explain the shock and the recovery with the same MA and AR terms that describe normal month-to-month behaviour, which pulls the coefficients away from their usual values. Simply deleting the COVID months is not possible, because an ARIMA model needs equally spaced observations.
Two designs are used. Design B is the main analysis; Design A is a sensitivity check that shows what happens if the break is ignored.

Design B, main analysis (COVID as missing): replace March 2020 to March 2022 by NA. ARIMA() in fable can evaluate the likelihood when some observations are missing: the missing months simply contribute nothing to it. The parameters are therefore estimated only from the pre-COVID and post-COVID months, while the monthly time ordering (which the lag structure of the model depends on) is kept intact. The benchmark methods also cope with missing values (for example, seasonal naive uses the last observed value for each month).
Design A, sensitivity check (COVID kept): fit every model to the observed series, including the COVID months.

The letters are kept from the order in which the designs were first set up; throughout the report, B is the design the conclusions rest on.
This is a deliberately simple treatment of the break. A more structural treatment with intervention variables is left for Project 3.

4.3 Training and test sets


Code
train_A <- nights_sold |> filter(Month < test_start)
train_B <- train_A |>
  mutate(nights = if_else(period == "COVID window", NA_real_, nights))

design_levels <- c("A (sensitivity): COVID kept", "B (main): COVID as missing")

train <- bind_rows(
  as_tibble(train_A) |> mutate(design = design_levels[1]),
  as_tibble(train_B) |> mutate(design = design_levels[2])
) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Month, key = design)

# Full observed series with the design key, used for accuracy() so that
# both designs are scored against the same actual values and the MASE
# uses the same scaling for both designs.
nights_keyed <- bind_rows(
  as_tibble(nights_sold) |> mutate(design = design_levels[1]),
  as_tibble(nights_sold) |> mutate(design = design_levels[2])
) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Month, key = design)


The models are trained on January 2015 to June 2024 (114 months, of which 25 are set to missing in Design B) and tested on July 2024 to June 2026 (24 months). A two year test set covers two full seasonal cycles, so every calendar month is forecast twice, at short and long horizons.

Why these models. The four benchmarks are the standard set from the notes. Seasonal naive is the one that matters most: because the seasonal shape is so stable (Figure 2), simply repeating last year’s value is a hard target, and any ARIMA model has to beat it to justify its extra parameters. The ARMA and non-seasonal ARIMA models are deliberately misspecified reference points rather than serious candidates. The ARMA has no differencing and no seasonal terms, and the ARIMA handles the level but not the seasonality. Including them shows how much each feature of the data (the wandering level, then the seasonality) contributes to forecast accuracy. The real candidates are the two seasonal models: the hand identified airline model from the ACF and PACF, and the automatic ARIMA() choice as a check on the hand identification.
The differencing orders are fixed from the identification step rather than chosen by unit root tests inside ARIMA(), so that both designs use the same differencing and the comparison isolates the effect of the COVID treatment. Point forecasts from the log scale models are back-transformed with the bias adjustment that fable applies by default, so they are forecasts of the mean rather than the median.

text:
5.1 Selected orders and information criteria

Under Design A the residual plot is dominated by a handful of enormous residuals in 2020 (the largest is 8.9 standard deviations from zero), so the normality assumption behind the prediction intervals fails badly, even though the Ljung and Box test (p = 0.912) does not detect autocorrelation. Under Design B the airline residuals look like white noise (p = 0.140), and the histogram is roughly symmetric. Two spikes in the residual ACF (Figure 10), at lags 9 and 18, just cross the 95% bounds. With 36 lags about two exceedances are expected by chance and the Ljung and Box test does not reject, so the model is accepted; but lag 9 also stood out in the identification step, so it is noted as a limitation. The ARMA model without differencing leaves strong autocorrelation in its residuals under Design B (p = 0.000), which is expected: it has no way to represent the seasonal pattern.
Applying step 6 of the procedure. Under Design B the models that pass the white noise test are: SARIMA (0,1,1)(0,1,1), SARIMA (auto). The models that fail are: ARIMA, ARMA. For a model that fails, the procedure says to return to step 4 rather than forecast. For the ARMA and non-seasonal ARIMA models, returning to step 4 means recognising from their residual ACF that the seasonal autocorrelation has not been modelled, which leads straight to the seasonal models. The automatically selected SARIMA passes as well, but only just (p = 0.051, right at the 5% cut-off), so it remains a candidate alongside the hand identified model, with weaker support. Under Design A every model technically passes the Ljung and Box test, but the airline model fails step 6 in a different way: its residuals are far from identically distributed (the COVID residuals are extreme outliers) and its seasonal MA coefficient sits on the invertibility boundary. Returning to step 4 under Design A would not fix this, because the problem is the data, not the orders. The fix is to change how the break is handled, which is what Design B does.
Candidates for the final model. Only the models that pass the loop under Design B are candidates for forecasting. The test set comparison below then checks the last condition from the notes: whether these candidates beat the benchmarks.

title: Project 1: Forecasting South African Accommodation Demand with ARIMA and SARIMA Models
text:
9.1 Key findings

Seasonality is the dominant and most stable feature of the series. The seasonal shape barely changed even through the COVID years, which is why the seasonal naive method is hard to beat. The non-seasonal ARMA and ARIMA models cannot represent the seasonal pattern and fail the residual diagnostics; the ARMA happened to score reasonably on the test set, but not for reasons that would carry over to other periods.
How the break is handled matters more than which ARIMA model is chosen. With the COVID months kept (Design A), the seasonal ARIMA models were worse than the seasonal naive benchmark on the test set and much worse in cross-validation. The cause is a residual variance inflated by about 134 times, a seasonal MA coefficient pushed to the invertibility boundary (-1.000), and point forecasts pushed upwards by the bias adjustment.
With the COVID window treated as missing (Design B), the Box and Jenkins airline model was the only model to pass the full loop and beat the benchmarks: it passed the diagnostic step and performed best, with a test RMSE of 101.6 thousand nights (MAPE 4.25%), white noise residuals and slightly conservative prediction intervals (the 80% intervals covered 92% of test months and the 95% intervals all of them). It also had the lowest cross-validated error at every horizon from 1 to 12 months.
A lower AICc did not guarantee better forecasts. The automatically selected seasonal model had a lower AICc than the hand identified model but higher test RMSE, so the simpler model identified from the ACF and PACF was preferred.

title: Project 1: Forecasting South African Accommodation Demand with ARIMA and SARIMA Models
text:
9.2 Issues and limitations

Choice of COVID window. The window (March 2020 to March 2022) follows the national state of disaster. The data suggest the recovery continued after April 2022, so some post-COVID months still carry the recovery trend into the training data. A sensitivity check with a window ending in December 2022 would test how much this matters.
Treating the shock as missing discards information. Setting 25 months to missing throws away real data, and the approach would not work for a shock at the very end of a series. An intervention model (a level shift or a ramp with a gradual recovery) would use those months instead of ignoring them; this is the starting point for Project 3.
Transformation. The log was used for interpretability; a Box–Cox transformation with the Guerrero \(\hat\lambda\) could be compared as a check.
Level shift after COVID. Demand has recovered to slightly below its pre-COVID level. The differenced models adapt to this because they forecast from the most recent level, but the mean benchmark does not. Under Design A it only did reasonably well because the COVID months drag the long-run average down close to the recovered level; under Design B, without those months, its average sits well above the test data and it is among the worst methods.
Residual autocorrelation at lag 9. The airline residuals pass the Ljung and Box test, but lag 9 crosses the bounds both before fitting and in the residuals. It has no obvious calendar explanation and adding a lag 9 term would be hard to justify, so it is left unmodelled.
MASE scaling. The MASE denominator uses an in-sample period that contains the COVID collapse, so the MASE values are deflated. RMSE and MAPE were used as the main measures.
Bias adjustment. Back-transforming with the mean (bias adjusted) forecast is the right choice when the forecasts are added up, for example into annual totals, but it makes the forecasts very sensitive to an inflated \(\hat\sigma^2\). This was a large part of the failure of Design A and is easy to miss.
Short post-COVID history. Only about two years of post-COVID data are in the training set, and the test set is two years long, so the conclusions rest on a fairly short stretch of “normal” data.

text:
9.3 What I would do differently
I would model the COVID shock directly with intervention variables in a regression with ARIMA errors, so that the 25 months are used rather than discarded. Project 3 takes up this idea on the same series and the same test set, which allows a direct comparison with the SARIMA results from this project. I would also compare a sliding window with the expanding window in the cross-validation, since a sliding window is the natural choice when structural breaks are plausible.

title: Project 1: Forecasting South African Accommodation Demand with ARIMA and SARIMA Models
text:
9.4 Project reflections and development
When I first started thinking about the best way to approach this problem I was very intrigued by the idea of using financial data. I immediately found some data online and had AI do a mini analysis of the data with SARIMA, ARIMA and the other models present in this project. I quickly found that the analysis would not yield the kind of results I wanted because of the volatility and variation within financial stock data. I therefore pivoted and went back and forth on a couple of different econometric datasets. I had the idea to use the Airbnb dataset that I had worked with earlier in the year during a data analytics course but unfortunately the data was not able to be processed in a time series way. Therefore, using the assistance of AI I was able to track down and pull data from the Stats SA website about tourist accommodation, a dataset that would fit and perform much more consistently with AR, MA, ARIMA and SARIMA models.
Upon looking at the EDA this data showed a clear seasonal pattern with a unique drop in 2020 due to the COVID pandemic as well as clear signs of non-stationarity. This also changed the way I wanted to approach the project because I first wanted to start with fitting an AR and an MA model and then build up to ARMA and then ARIMA and SARIMA. This idea quickly disappeared when the EDA showed clear signs of non-stationarity and variability. I therefore decided to shift the focus of my project onto ARIMA and SARIMA modelling and the process of differencing.
I found that this data was quite similar to a seasonally adjusted electrical equipment dataset that was covered in one of the coding lectures. This is due to the fact that both datasets had a level of non-stationarity and the variability mostly occurred due to a shock at a specific time. For this dataset it was COVID and for the other dataset it was the 2008/2009 crash. In that example the crash caused a sharp drop and a slow recovery that a single ARIMA model struggled to describe, which is exactly the problem COVID created here, so seeing it in the lecture first helped me recognise the issue in my own data
The biggest thing I learned from this project is how much a single structural break can damage a model that otherwise looks reasonable. When I kept the COVID months in, the airline model still passed the Ljung–Box test, and at first I took that as a sign the model was fine. Only when I looked at the residual plot and the forecasts did I see that a handful of residuals from 2020 had inflated the variance by more than 100 times, pushed the seasonal MA coefficient to -1 and made the forecasts and intervals useless. This taught me that a white noise test only checks whether the residuals are correlated, not whether they are well behaved, so the diagnostic step has to include actually looking at the residuals and not just reading off a p-value.
The part I found most difficult was making decisions when the evidence disagreed. The unit root tests said no first difference was needed while the ACF and the time plot suggested one was, the Guerrero estimate pointed to a different transformation from the log I had chosen, and the automatic model had a better AICc than my hand-identified model but forecast worse on the test set. Earlier in the course I would have just followed whichever test or criterion the software gave me. Working through these cases made me understand that the modelling procedure is a set of judgement calls, and that the important thing is to explain why I made each choice and then check it afterwards, for example by confirming that the fitted MA coefficient was not close to -1 and that the seasonal MA term was clearly significant.
I also reworked the project part way through so that it follows the seven-step ARIMA procedure from the lectures, with the COVID months treated as missing as the main analysis and keeping them only as a sensitivity check. This made the report much easier to follow, because every decision now sits under a clear step, and it made me see the procedure as a loop rather than a straight line: a model that fails the residual check sends you back to the identification step instead of straight to forecasting.
I used AI throughout this project to help me find the data, debug my code and review my write-up, and these uses are recorded in my AI use log. The review in particular picked up places where my text did not match my own output, such as describing an autocorrelation as negative when it was positive. Going back through each of these against my tables and plots was a useful lesson in checking that every claim in a report is actually supported by the results.
Going forward, the main thing I want to explore is handling the COVID shock directly instead of setting those months to missing, since treating them as missing throws away two years of real data. That is the starting point for Project 3, where I model the shock with intervention variables on the same series and test set so the results can be compared directly with this project.

text:
NoteExecutive summary



Title: Time series regression and exponential smoothing for South African accommodation demand
Section and topic: Section 2. Time series regression (trend, seasonal dummies and Fourier terms, intervention variables, a predictor series, regression with ARIMA errors) and exponential smoothing (simple, Holt, damped trend, Holt–Winters and the ETS framework).
Type of project: Implementation and model comparison on real-world data. I code the additive Holt–Winters method from first principles (the recursions and the least squares estimation) and check it against ETS() in fable. The project uses the same series and the same test set as Project 1, so the results of the two projects can be compared directly.
Question: How well do the two main Section 2 forecasting approaches, time series regression and exponential smoothing, forecast monthly accommodation demand, and how should each of them deal with the COVID-19 collapse? Can either of them beat the Project 1 SARIMA model?
Data: Real-world, publicly available data. Statistics South Africa, Tourist Accommodation release P6410, series B64100 (stay unit nights sold, total industry), and the monthly average rand per US dollar exchange rate (FRED series EXSFUS), January 2015 to June 2026. Full source details are in Section 2.1.
Methods: Regression: a static regression with trend, seasonal dummies and COVID intervention terms, then a regression with ARIMA errors in which the intervention decay rate is chosen by profile likelihood, the seasonal form (dummies or Fourier terms) by AICc and the error model by the Box and Jenkins steps; the log exchange rate is added and forecast both ex ante and ex post. Exponential smoothing: ETS on the raw training data, then the full family of exponential smoothing methods on a series in which the COVID window is replaced by regression-based imputed values, with my own Holt–Winters code as a check, and, as a further check, the same models fitted to the post-COVID years only. All models are diagnosed (Ljung and Box) and compared with the seasonal naive benchmark and the Project 1 SARIMA on the July 2024 to June 2026 test set and by rolling-origin cross-validation.
Key findings: A static regression fits the training data closely (adjusted \(R^2\) = 0.965), but its errors are strongly autocorrelated, so its standard errors and intervals cannot be trusted. Letting the errors follow an ARIMA(2,1,1) process fixes this and describes the COVID shock with five parameters (a decaying shock with a half-life of about 2.5 months, two pulses and a level shift), giving a test RMSE of 98.8 against 101.6 for the Project 1 SARIMA. The exchange rate does not improve realistic forecasts. Exponential smoothing breaks on the raw data, where the level smoothing parameter goes to 1, but works once the COVID window is imputed: the damped Holt–Winters model was the most accurate model on the test set (RMSE 72.5), while the Project 1 SARIMA remained the best in rolling-origin cross-validation. Details are in Section 7.1.
What I would do differently: Add noise to the imputed COVID values (multiple imputation) so that the exponential smoothing models do not treat them as exact, and estimate the intervention decay rate jointly with the other regression parameters rather than on a grid.
Detailed analysis: the sections below.

text:
3.1 Describing the COVID shock with intervention variables
A regression can absorb the shock if it is given explanatory variables whose shape matches how the event unfolded. This follows the transfer function idea from the notes. With \(t_0\) = April 2020 and everything on the log scale:

Decaying shock: \(D_t(\delta) = \delta^{\,t - t_0}\) for \(t \ge t_0\) and 0 before. Its coefficient \(\omega\) is the immediate effect in April 2020, which then dies out geometrically at rate \(\delta\). This is the transfer function \(\omega / (1 - \delta L)\) applied to a pulse at \(t_0\).
Pulses for March 2020 (lockdown started on 27 March, so the month was only partly affected) and May 2020 (the industry stayed almost completely closed, so the bottom of the collapse lasted two months rather than one).
Level shift: \(S_t = 1\) for \(t \ge t_0\), allowing a permanent difference between the pre-COVID and post-COVID levels.



Code
covid_vars <- function(df, delta) {
  k0 <- month_num(shock_month)
  df |>
    mutate(k     = month_num(Month) - k0,
           decay = if_else(k >= 0, delta^pmax(k, 0), 0),
           mar20 = as.numeric(k == -1),
           may20 = as.numeric(k == 1),
           step  = as.numeric(k >= 0))
}

3.2 Model A1: static regression
The simplest time series regression (fpp3 Chapter 7) has a linear trend, 11 seasonal dummies and the intervention variables, with independent errors:
\[
\log y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t + \sum_{j=2}^{12} \gamma_j M_{jt} + \omega D_t(\delta) + \kappa_1 P^{\text{Mar20}}_t + \kappa_2 P^{\text{May20}}_t + \lambda S_t + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t \overset{iid}{\sim} N(0, \sigma^2).
\]
\(\delta\) is fixed at a provisional value of 0.80 here; it is chosen properly in Section 3.3.1.


Code
train_static <- covid_vars(train, 0.80)
test_static  <- covid_vars(test, 0.80)

fit_static <- train_static |>
  model(TSLM(log(nights) ~ trend() + season() + decay + mar20 + may20 + step))

static_glance <- glance(fit_static)
static_res    <- augment(fit_static)$.innov
dw_static     <- sum(diff(static_res)^2) / sum(static_res^2)          # Durbin-Watson
lb_static     <- Box.test(static_res, lag = 24, type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value
r1_static     <- acf(static_res, lag.max = 1, plot = FALSE)$acf[2]




Code
fit_static |> gg_tsresiduals(lag_max = 36)








Figure 2: Residual diagnostics for the static regression (Model A1).





The fit looks impressive: the adjusted \(R^2\) is 0.965. The residuals tell a different story (Figure 2). They drift in long runs above and below zero, the lag 1 autocorrelation is 0.73, the Durbin–Watson statistic is 0.53 (far below the value of 2 expected for independent errors) and the Ljung and Box test on 24 lags gives p < 0.001.
This matters for more than tidiness. With positively autocorrelated errors, the least squares estimates are still unbiased but no longer efficient, the reported standard errors are too small, so the intervention terms look more significant than they are, and the prediction intervals are too narrow. The static regression also ignores useful information: if this month was above the fitted line, next month probably will be too. The remedy, following fpp3 Chapter 10, is to let the error follow an ARIMA process.

title: Project 3: Time Series Regression and Exponential Smoothing for South African Accommodation Demand
section: 3.3 Model A2: regression with ARIMA errors
text:
3.3 Model A2: regression with ARIMA errors
The dynamic regression replaces the independent error by an ARIMA process:
\[
\log y_t = \sum_{j=2}^{12} \gamma_j M_{jt} + \omega D_t(\delta) + \kappa_1 P^{\text{Mar20}}_t + \kappa_2 P^{\text{May20}}_t + \lambda S_t + \eta_t, \qquad (1 - L)\,\phi(L)\,\eta_t = \theta(L)\,\varepsilon_t .
\]
Two choices from the static model are revisited. First, the deterministic trend is dropped in favour of a first difference in the errors: after the shock the level does not follow a straight line, and a wandering (stochastic) level is more realistic. With \(d = 1\) the intercept and trend are differenced away, which is why they do not appear. Second, the seasonality is kept deterministic (dummies) rather than handled with a seasonal difference. In Project 1, the airline model fitted with the COVID months included estimated a seasonal MA coefficient of -1.000. A seasonal MA factor \((1 - L^{12})\) that cancels the seasonal difference is the classic sign that the seasonal pattern is fixed rather than evolving, so that seasonal differencing is over-differencing. The seasonal plots in Project 1 point the same way, and the exponential smoothing models below confirm it independently: every seasonal ETS model puts the seasonal smoothing parameter \(\gamma\) at or near its lower bound, so the seasonal pattern barely changes over ten years.

3.3.1 Choosing the decay rate by profile likelihood
The decay rate \(\delta\) enters the model non-linearly, so it cannot be estimated by ARIMA() directly. Instead I profile it: for each \(\delta\) on a grid from 0.70 to 0.96, the model is fitted (with the ARIMA error orders chosen by AICc) and the AICc recorded. The value of \(\delta\) with the smallest AICc is used. Because \(\delta\) is estimated, the model really has one more parameter than ARIMA() reports; this does not change the ranking along the grid.


Code
delta_grid <- seq(0.70, 0.96, by = 0.02)

profile <- bind_rows(lapply(delta_grid, function(dl) {
  f <- covid_vars(train, dl) |>
    model(reg = ARIMA(log(nights) ~ season() + decay + mar20 + may20 + step +
                        pdq(d = 1) + PDQ(0, 0, 0)))
  tibble(delta = dl,
         AICc  = glance(f)$AICc,
         spec  = format(f$reg[[1]]))
}))

delta_hat <- profile$delta[which.min(profile$AICc)]




Code
ggplot(profile, aes(delta, AICc)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(data = filter(profile, delta == delta_hat), colour = "firebrick", size = 3) +
  labs(x = expression(delta), y = "AICc")








Figure 3: Profile of AICc against the decay rate. The selected value is marked in red.





The AICc is minimised at \(\hat\delta\) = 0.76 (Figure 3). A decay rate of 0.76 means that the temporary part of the shock halves every 2.5 months and has fallen to 4% of its initial size after a year.


3.3.2 Seasonal dummies or Fourier terms?
Fourier terms (\(\sin(2\pi k t/12)\) and \(\cos(2\pi k t/12)\) for \(k = 1, \dots, K\)) are the other standard way to put seasonality into a regression. With small \(K\) they describe a smooth seasonal shape with fewer parameters; with \(K = 6\) they are equivalent to the 11 dummies. I compare the two at \(\hat\delta\) by AICc. All the models have the same response and the same order of differencing, so their AICc values are comparable.

The selected error model is LM w/ ARIMA(2,1,1) errors. The estimates have a direct interpretation on the log scale. The decaying shock has \(\hat\omega\) = -3.19; combined with the May 2020 pulse and the level shift, this reproduces a loss of almost all demand in April and May 2020. The level shift is \(\hat\lambda\) = -0.515 (p < 0.001). This needs careful interpretation. Because the error \(\eta_t\) has a unit root, it has its own wandering level, and the slow two-year recovery is carried by the error rather than by the intervention terms: the decaying shock dies out quickly (see the half-life above), and \(\hat\lambda\) is the part of the April 2020 drop that did not decay geometrically. It is therefore not the gap between the pre- and post-COVID levels; that gap is estimated directly in Section 4.2. Figure 5 shows the contribution of the intervention terms alone, which is why it stays flat after 2020; the recovery towards the post-COVID level happens in the error process.   as_tibble() |>
  left_join(n_arma, by = ".model") |>
  mutate(dof = coalesce(dof, 0L)) |>
  group_by(.model) |>
  summarise(lb_p = Box.test(.innov, lag = 24, type = "Ljung-Box",
                            fitdf = first(dof))$p.value,
            .groups = "drop")

lbp <- function(m) reg_lb$lb_p[reg_lb$.model == m]

The innovations of the regression model are consistent with white noise and show no remaining seasonal structure, so the deterministic seasonal dummies are adequate. Compared with the static regression, the long runs in the residuals have disappeared: the ARIMA error has absorbed the autocorrelation. The model passes the residual check (step 6) and can be used to forecast.

section: 3.4 Model A3: adding the exchange rate
text:
3.4 Model A3: adding the exchange rate
Because the model is in logs, the coefficient on log USD/ZAR is an elasticity: a 10% weakening of the rand is associated with a change of about 2.7% in nights sold, holding the seasonal and COVID terms fixed. The estimate is 0.270 (p 0.175), and the AICc gets worse from -227.1 to -225.9. The exchange rate does not add significant information once the seasonal pattern and the COVID shock are accounted for, which is not surprising since most stays are domestic and the effect of the rand on foreign arrivals works with a lag. The errors are differenced, so the coefficient is identified from changes in the rand and changes in demand within the same month.
A regression with a predictor series has a practical catch: to forecast nights sold, I need future values of the exchange rate, which are not known when the forecast is made. Two versions are therefore evaluated:

Ex ante (realistic): the exchange rate is assumed to stay at its last observed value (June 2024), a naive forecast.
Ex post (optimistic): the actual exchange rate during the test period is used. This is not a genuine forecast, since it uses information that would not have been available in June 2024. It shows the best the model could do if the rand were forecast perfectly.

text:
4.1 Model B1: ETS on the raw training data
The ETS() function selects the error, trend and seasonal forms (additive, multiplicative or none) by AICc and estimates the smoothing parameters and initial states by maximum likelihood. Exponential smoothing cannot skip missing observations, so the first attempt simply fits ETS to the training data including the COVID months, on both the original and the log scale.


Code
fit_ets_raw <- train |>
  model(`ETS raw (original scale)` = ETS(nights),
        `ETS raw (log scale)`      = ETS(log(nights)))

ets_par_tbl <- function(fit) {
  tidy(fit) |>
    filter(term %in% c("alpha", "beta", "gamma", "phi")) |>
    select(.model, term, estimate) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = term, values_from = estimate) |>
    left_join(tibble(.model = names(fit),
                     Form = vapply(names(fit), function(m) format(fit[[m]][[1]]), "")),
              by = ".model") |>
    relocate(Form, .after = .model)
}

alpha_raw <- raw_tbl$alpha

This is the exponential smoothing version of the problem Project 1 had with SARIMA. On both scales the level smoothing parameter is at its upper limit (\(\hat\alpha \approx\) 1.000): the only way the method can follow a collapse of more than 95% and a two-year recovery is to reset the level to the latest observation every month. On the log scale the selected model even has no seasonal component: on the log scale the April 2020 drop is many times larger than the seasonal swings, so the likelihood gains nothing from tracking the season. A model with no seasonality for a series this seasonal is clearly wrong. With \(\alpha = 1\) the forecasts are simply the last observation (plus the seasonal pattern, if there is one), the residual variance is inflated by the COVID months and the prediction intervals are very wide. The COVID window has to be dealt with before exponential smoothing can work.

title: Project 3: Time Series Regression and Exponential Smoothing for South African Accommodation Demand
section: 4.2 Imputing the COVID window with a regression
text:
4.2 Imputing the COVID window with a regression
Three ways of handling the window are possible: (1) fit only to the post-COVID months, which leaves just over two years of data to estimate 12 seasonal effects (tested as a check in Section 4.5); (2) remove the estimated intervention effect from Part A; or (3) replace the COVID months by values that describe what demand would have looked like without the pandemic. Option (2) does not help much: the regression explains the shock partly through its ARIMA error, so the “adjusted” series still contains most of the recovery dynamics. I therefore use option (3), with a regression as the imputation model.
The imputation regression is fitted only to the non-COVID months:
\[
\log y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t + \sum_{j=2}^{12} \gamma_j M_{jt} + \lambda R_t + \varepsilon_t,
\]
where \(R_t\) is a ramp: 0 before March 2020, 1 after March 2022, and rising linearly through the window. Since \(R_t\) only takes the values 0 and 1 in the months used for fitting, \(\lambda\) is the difference between the pre- and post-COVID levels; inside the window the ramp produces a straight-line transition between the two levels, with the usual seasonal pattern on top. The fitted values in the window are used as the imputed values.


Code
impute_covid <- function(df) {
  n_win <- month_num(covid_end) - month_num(covid_start) + 2
  df <- df |>
    as_tibble() |>
    mutate(t      = row_number(),
           mon    = factor(month(as.Date(Month))),
           in_win = Month >= covid_start & Month <= covid_end,
           ramp   = pmin(pmax((month_num(Month) - month_num(covid_start) + 1) / n_win, 0), 1),
           y_obs  = if_else(in_win, NA_real_, log(nights)))
  fit <- lm(y_obs ~ t + mon + ramp, data = df)   # lm drops the NA months
  df |>
    mutate(log_fit     = predict(fit, newdata = df),
           nights_imp  = if_else(in_win, exp(log_fit), nights)) |>
    select(-t, -mon, -y_obs, -log_fit) |>
    structure(imputation_fit = fit)          # keep the fitted model for reporting
}

train_imp_tbl <- impute_covid(train)
imp_lm        <- attr(train_imp_tbl, "imputation_fit")
train_imp     <- train_imp_tbl |> as_tsibble(index = Month)

imp_r2   <- summary(imp_lm)$r.squared
imp_ramp <- coef(imp_lm)[["ramp"]]




Code
train_imp |>
  ggplot(aes(as.Date(Month))) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = as.Date(covid_start), xmax = as.Date(covid_end),
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, alpha = 0.15, fill = "firebrick") +
  geom_line(aes(y = nights), colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(aes(y = nights_imp), colour = "firebrick", linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Nights sold (thousands)")








Figure 7: Training data on the original scale (grey) and the series used for exponential smoothing, in which the COVID window (shaded) is replaced by the regression-imputed values (red).





The imputation regression explains 94.8% of the variation in the non-COVID months, and the estimated difference between the post- and pre-COVID levels is -0.212 on the log scale (-19.1%). This is the clearest estimate in the project of how far demand remains below its pre-COVID path. It is much smaller than the level shift in the regression with ARIMA errors (\(\hat\lambda\) = -0.515), which confirms the point made there: in that model the error process carries part of the recovery, so \(\hat\lambda\) is not the long-run gap. The imputed values (Figure 7) carry the seasonal pattern smoothly across the gap. Their weakness is that they contain no noise, which I return to in the discussion.

section: 4.3 Model B2: Holt–Winters from first principles
text:
4.3 Model B2: Holt–Winters from first principles
To make sure I understand what ETS() is doing, I implement the additive Holt–Winters method myself (fpp3 Section 8.3). With \(y_t\) the log of the imputed series, \(\ell_t\) the level, \(b_t\) the trend and \(s_t\) the seasonal effect, the one-step forecast and the error are
\[
\hat y_{t \mid t-1} = \ell_{t-1} + b_{t-1} + s_{t-12}, \qquad e_t = y_t - \hat y_{t \mid t-1},
\]
and the components are updated in error-correction form:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\ell_t &= \ell_{t-1} + b_{t-1} + \alpha e_t, \\
b_t    &= b_{t-1} + \beta e_t, \\
s_t    &= s_{t-12} + \gamma e_t .
\end{aligned}
\]
Each update moves a component in the direction of the latest error, and the smoothing parameters say how far. The \(h\)-step forecast is \(\hat y_{T+h \mid T} = \ell_T + h\, b_T + s_{T+h-12k}\), where \(k\) makes the seasonal index refer to the last observed year. With additive errors, maximising the Gaussian likelihood is the same as minimising the sum of squared one-step errors (the error variance can be profiled out), so I estimate the three smoothing parameters and the 13 free initial states (\(\ell_0\), \(b_0\) and 11 seasonal effects; the 12th is set so the seasonal effects sum to zero) by minimising the SSE with optim(). The parameter bounds match those in fable (between 0.0001 and 0.9999).


Code
# Additive Holt-Winters filter -------------------------------------------
# par = (alpha, beta, gamma, l0, b0, s_{-11}, ..., s_{-1});
# the last seasonal state s_0 makes the 12 initial effects sum to zero.
hw_filter <- function(par, y, m = 12) {
  alpha <- par[1]; beta <- par[2]; gamma <- par[3]
  level <- par[4]; trend <- par[5]
  s     <- c(par[6:(4 + m)], -sum(par[6:(4 + m)]))  # s[1] is the effect for the next month
  n <- length(y); e <- yhat <- numeric(n)
  for (t in 1:n) {
    yhat[t] <- level + trend + s[1]
    e[t]    <- y[t] - yhat[t]
    new_level <- level + trend + alpha * e[t]
    trend     <- trend + beta * e[t]
    s         <- c(s[-1], s[1] + gamma * e[t])        # rotate the seasonal states
    level     <- new_level
  }
  list(e = e, fitted = yhat, level = level, trend = trend, season = s)
}

hw_forecast <- function(state, h, m = 12) {
  state$level + (1:h) * state$trend + rep(state$season, length.out = h)
}

# Estimation by least squares --------------------------------------------
y_imp <- log(train_imp$nights_imp)
sse   <- function(par) sum(hw_filter(par, y_imp)$e^2)

# Starting values: classical decomposition of the first two years
first2 <- y_imp[1:24]
s_init <- y_imp[1:12] - mean(y_imp[1:12])
start  <- c(0.3, 0.01, 0.1,
            mean(first2[1:12]), (mean(first2[13:24]) - mean(first2[1:12])) / 12,
            (s_init - mean(s_init))[1:11])

own_opt <- optim(start, sse, method = "L-BFGS-B",
                 lower = c(rep(1e-4, 3), rep(-Inf, 13)),
                 upper = c(rep(0.9999, 3), rep(Inf, 13)),
                 control = list(maxit = 10000))
own_hw  <- hw_filter(own_opt$par, y_imp)

# The same model in fable --------------------------------------------------
fit_hw_fable <- train_imp |>
  model(HW = ETS(log(nights_imp) ~ error("A") + trend("A") + season("A")))
fable_par <- tidy(fit_hw_fable)
fable_sse <- sum(augment(fit_hw_fable)$.innov^2)
fp <- function(t) fable_par$estimate[fable_par$term == t]

My optimiser actually reaches a slightly lower SSE (0.08502 against 0.08541), so the small differences in the parameters come from the two optimisers stopping at different points on a very flat surface, not from a difference in the model. text:
4.4 Model B3: the exponential smoothing family on the imputed series
With the window imputed, the full family from fpp3 Chapter 8 can be fitted to the log series. AICc can be used to compare these models because they all have the same response and none of them is differenced.


Code
fit_ets <- train_imp |>
  model(
    SES                 = ETS(log(nights_imp) ~ error("A") + trend("N")  + season("N")),
    Holt                = ETS(log(nights_imp) ~ error("A") + trend("A")  + season("N")),

4.5 Model B4: a check using the post-COVID years only
The imputation approach keeps all ten years of data but fills the COVID window with values that were never observed. A simpler alternative is to drop everything before April 2022 and fit exponential smoothing only to the post-COVID months. At first sight little should be lost, because exponential smoothing already gives the most weight to the latest observations. That is true for the level, but not for the other components here. In the models above, \(\gamma\) and \(\beta\) sit at or near their lower bounds, so the seasonal pattern and the slope are hardly updated at all: they stay close to their initial values, which are estimated from the whole series back to 2015. The early years therefore still shape the seasonal pattern and the trend, however small their weight in the level. Fitting to the post-COVID months only is the one way to let those components reflect current behaviour. The cost is data: April 2022 to June 2024 gives just 27 months to estimate up to four smoothing parameters and 13 initial states.


Code
post_start <- yearmonth("2022 Apr")

    `Holt-Winters` = ETS(log(nights) ~ error("A") + trend("A")  + season("A")),

What happens with less data. With only 27 months, each seasonal effect is effectively estimated from two or three values. Across the three post-COVID fits (Table 6), the level parameter ranges from \(\hat\alpha\) = 0.000 to 0.844, and the largest seasonal parameter is \(\hat\gamma\) = 0.0028. As on the full series, the seasonal pattern is held essentially fixed: two years of data contain no evidence that it is changing. The level parameter, in contrast, differs widely between the three forms, a sign that the short sample cannot pin down how quickly the level should adapt.
Forecast accuracy. On the test set (Table 7, Figure 9), the best of the post-COVID fits is Damped HW (RMSE 75.3), against 72.5 for the damped Holt–Winters model on the imputed series and 132.6 for seasonal naive. Dropping the earlier years helps Holt-Winters but not the other two, so the ranking of the three models changes with the training window. The ETS(A,N,A) model moves from an RMSE of 95.9 to 117.5, Holt–Winters from 151.7 to 80.7, and damped Holt–Winters from 72.5 to 75.3. With two years of data, the trend each model estimates comes from a very short stretch of the recovery, so which model forecasts best depends heavily on how that short-run slope happens to continue.
The large improvement for Holt–Winters shows where the problem with the undamped model on the imputed series lies. There, the slope is fixed at the value estimated for the start of the series in 2015, which is slightly negative, and it is extrapolated for two full years, so the forecasts drift steadily below the data (Figure 9). Fitted to the post-COVID months, the slope comes from the recovery instead, which happened to continue through the test period. But this version is not a better model so much as a different gamble. Its smoothing parameters are all close to zero (\(\hat\alpha\) = 0.0003), so it is essentially a fixed straight line plus a fixed seasonal pattern drawn through 27 months. Its 95% intervals are the narrowest of all (mean width 251 thousand nights), yet they still miss 12% of the test months.
The damped model is the most revealing result of the check. Fitted to completely different training windows, it gives almost the same forecast accuracy (RMSE 72.5 and 75.3), because damping makes the long-horizon forecast depend much less on exactly how the slope is estimated. That robustness is a stronger argument for the damped trend than its single best test-set score. The short window still has a cost: the damped model’s 95% intervals are wider when it is fitted to the post-COVID months only (mean width 813 against 543 thousand nights), reflecting the extra uncertainty in parameters estimated from two years of data.
Seasonal pattern. The seasonal effects learned from the post-COVID months alone are close to those from the full imputed series (Figure 10): the largest difference in any month is 2.9%. This confirms, from a different angle, the finding from Project 1 that the seasonal shape survived COVID unchanged, and it means that the long history is not distorting the seasonal pattern. Its value lies in pinning down the level and the trend, which is exactly where the short-window fits are least stable.
Conclusion of the check. Using only the post-COVID years avoids imputation entirely, and for some model forms it forecasts well. But the results are fragile: with so little data the outcome depends on the choice of trend, and there is no way to tell in advance which choice will work. The imputed series gives the models enough history to estimate the seasonal pattern and the trend reliably, which is why it remains the main approach in this project.

text:
5.2 Rolling-origin cross-validation
A single 24-month test set gives one realisation of each model’s forecast errors, so the ranking could be luck. As in Project 1, I also use an expanding window: the models are refitted at each of 13 origins from June 2024 to June 2025 and forecast 1 to 12 months ahead, and the errors are averaged by horizon. The imputation regression is refitted at every origin. To keep the computation manageable, the regression keeps \(\hat\delta\) and its ARIMA error orders fixed at the values chosen above; the ETS forms are also fixed, but all parameters are re-estimated. The exchange rate model is left out, since its ex ante forecasts would need a rand forecast at every origin. All the origins fall inside the test period, so the cross-validation is not independent of the test set; it checks whether the ranking holds when the forecast origin moves.


Code
reg_pdq <- fit_reg$Reg[[1]]$fit$spec
cv_origins <- 13
cv_h       <- 12

cv_data <- nights_sold |>
  stretch_tsibble(.init = nrow(train), .step = 1) |>
  filter(.id <= cv_origins)

cv_fc <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(cv_origins), function(i) {
  d   <- cv_data |> filter(.id == i) |> select(-.id)
  fut <- new_data(d, cv_h)

  # seasonal naive and Project 1 SARIMA
  dB <- d |> mutate(nights = if_else(period == "COVID window", NA_real_, nights))
  f1 <- forecast(d  |> model(`Seasonal naive` = SNAIVE(nights)), h = cv_h)
  f2 <- forecast(dB |> model(`SARIMA (Project 1)` =
                               ARIMA(log(nights) ~ 0 + pdq(0, 1, 1) + PDQ(0, 1, 1))), h = cv_h)

  # regression with ARIMA errors (orders fixed)
  dR <- covid_vars(d, delta_hat)
  fR <- covid_vars(fut, delta_hat)
  f3 <- forecast(dR |> model(Reg = ARIMA(log(nights) ~ season() + decay + mar20 + may20 + step +
                                           pdq(reg_pdq$p, 1, reg_pdq$q) + PDQ(0, 0, 0))),
                 new_data = fR)

  # exponential smoothing on the imputed series
  dI <- impute_covid(d) |> as_tsibble(index = Month)
  f4 <- forecast(dI |> model(
    `ETS(A,N,A)`   = ETS(log(nights_imp) ~ error("A") + trend("N")  + season("A")),
    `Holt-Winters` = ETS(log(nights_imp) ~ error("A") + trend("A")  + season("A")),
    `Damped HW`    = ETS(log(nights_imp) ~ error("A") + trend("Ad") + season("A"))),
    h = cv_h)

  bind_rows(as_tibble(f1), as_tibble(f2), as_tibble(f3), as_tibble(f4)) |>
    select(.model, Month, .mean) |>
    group_by(.model) |>
    mutate(h = row_number(), origin = i) |>
    ungroup()
})) |>
