title: Project 3: Time Series Regression and Exponential Smoothing for South African Accommodation Demand
text:
5.3 Results
Overall ranking. On the test set the lowest RMSE is achieved by the Damped HW model (72.5 thousand nights). Among the models that passed the diagnostic step, the best is Damped HW. For reference, the Project 1 SARIMA has an RMSE of 101.6 and the seasonal naive benchmark 132.6. In cross-validation the best model is SARIMA (Project 1) (RMSE 83.5), followed by Damped HW (89.5), with seasonal naive at 112.2 (Table 9, Figure 12). The two evaluations therefore do not fully agree, which is exactly why a single test set is not enough: the cross-validation forecasts start later (up to June 2025) and are at most 12 months ahead, so they reward models that track the recent level and penalise less for how the trend is extrapolated in the second year.
Static regression. The static regression has an RMSE of 233.8, worse than seasonal naive. Its deterministic trend is estimated from the whole training period, including the gentle decline before 2020, and is extrapolated through the test period, so the forecasts drift away from the data. Its 95% intervals happen to cover 100% of the test months, but only because the COVID months inflate the residual variance; with autocorrelated errors the interval formula itself is not valid, so this coverage cannot be relied on.
Regression with ARIMA errors. Modelling the error process gives an RMSE of 98.8 and a MAPE of 4.51%, better than the Project 1 SARIMA. Its intervals cover 100% of the test months at the 95% level and 100% at the 80% level, so they are too wide: a correct 80% interval should miss about one month in five. The reason is visible in Figure 6. The intervention terms capture the collapse but not every month of the uneven recovery, so the innovations in 2020 and 2021 are several times larger than normal and inflate the estimated error variance, which then widens every forecast interval (mean width 1,060 thousand nights against 545 for the SARIMA, which ignores those months). By June 2024 the temporary part of the shock had died out (\(\hat\delta^{\,50} \approx\) 1.1e-06), so the forecasts rest on the post-COVID level and the seasonal dummies. The main advantage of this model is interpretation: it estimates the size, shape and persistence of the shock (Figure 5) instead of discarding it.
Exchange rate. Adding the rand changes the RMSE to 106.2 ex ante and 130.3 ex post. Neither version improves on the model without the exchange rate, and the ex post version, which uses the actual exchange rate, is the worse of the two. The reason is the path of the rand. It strengthened from R18.43 per dollar in June 2024 to R16.39 by June 2026, and with a positive (but insignificant) elasticity the ex post model lowers its demand forecasts by about 3.1% by the end of the test period, while actual demand rose. The ex ante version holds the rand at its June 2024 value, so it avoids that drag. A regression’s forecasts are only as good as the forecasts (and the stability) of its explanatory variables.
Exponential smoothing on the raw data. ETS fitted with the COVID months included reaches an RMSE of 130.0, only just beating seasonal naive. With \(\hat\alpha = 1\) it is close to a seasonal random walk, and its 95% intervals are on average 2,292 thousand nights wide, against 1,060 for the regression.
Exponential smoothing on the imputed series. Imputing the window transforms exponential smoothing. The best of the seasonal models on the test set is Damped HW (RMSE 72.5), and the ranking among them is decided by the trend: the undamped Holt–Winters model (RMSE 151.7) extrapolates a fixed negative slope for two years, the no-trend model (RMSE 95.9) holds the level flat, and the damped model (RMSE 72.5) lets the slope fade. AICc preferred Holt-Winters, which is a useful reminder that AICc measures one-step-ahead fit in the training data, while the test set measures forecasts up to 24 months ahead, where the treatment of the trend dominates. The undamped model’s intervals also cover only 88% of the test months at the 95% level: its forecasts drift away from the data while the intervals stay narrow, partly because the noise-free imputed months shrink the estimated error variance. SES, which ignores the season, is far behind (RMSE 225.9), confirming the diagnostics.

title: Project 3: Time Series Regression and Exponential Smoothing for South African Accommodation Demand
text:
7.1 Key findings

A static regression is not enough. Trend, seasonal dummies and intervention terms give an adjusted \(R^2\) of 0.965, but the residuals are strongly autocorrelated (Durbin–Watson 0.53), so the standard errors and intervals cannot be trusted. Its test RMSE was 233.8.
Regression with ARIMA errors fixes this. With deterministic seasonal dummies (preferred to Fourier terms by AICc), a decaying intervention with \(\hat\delta\) = 0.76 (half-life about 2.5 months), two pulses and a level shift, the innovations are white noise (Ljung and Box p = 0.556), and the test RMSE is 98.8 against 101.6 for the Project 1 SARIMA. The shock is described with five parameters instead of 25 deleted months. The post-COVID level is estimated (by the imputation regression) to be 19% below the pre-COVID path.
The exchange rate had an estimated elasticity of 0.270 (p 0.175) and did not improve the realistic (ex ante) forecasts. Using the actual exchange rate made the forecasts worse, because the rand strengthened over the test period while demand rose.
Exponential smoothing breaks on the raw data. With the COVID months included, the level smoothing parameter goes to 1 and, on the log scale, AICc even drops the seasonal component.
Regression imputation rescues exponential smoothing. On the imputed series the seasonal models pass the diagnostics, and Damped HW reached a test RMSE of 72.5. The trend assumption (none, linear or damped) is what separates the seasonal models over a two-year horizon.
My own Holt–Winters code reproduces ETS(). The SSE agrees to 0.46% and both put \(\beta\) and \(\gamma\) at the boundary, confirming a fixed seasonal pattern and slope.
Using only the post-COVID years (Section 4.5) avoids imputation, but leaves just 27 months. The best exponential smoothing model fitted to that window was Damped HW (test RMSE 75.3), against 72.5 for damped Holt–Winters on the imputed series. Across the three trend forms the post-COVID RMSE ranged from 75.3 to 117.5, so with so little data the result depends heavily on the choice of trend. The damped model was the only one whose accuracy barely changed between the two training windows, which makes it the most robust choice.
Overall, the best model on the test set was Damped HW, the best that also passed the diagnostics was Damped HW, and the best in cross-validation was SARIMA (Project 1). Among the Section 2 models, Damped HW was the most accurate in cross-validation, so the Project 1 SARIMA remains a very strong benchmark: regression and exponential smoothing match it, but only beat it clearly on one of the two evaluations.

title: Project 3: Time Series Regression and Exponential Smoothing for South African Accommodation Demand
text:
7.2 Issues and limitations

The imputed values are treated as data. Exponential smoothing sees the 25 imputed months as exact observations with no noise. This makes the estimated error variance too small (so the intervals are too narrow) and can pull the smoothing parameters, since the imputed stretch is perfectly smooth. Multiple imputation (adding resampled residuals to the imputed values and averaging over many fits) would address this.
The imputation model is a modelling choice. The linear ramp between the pre- and post-COVID levels is a simple assumption. A different path (for example a faster or slower recovery) would change the imputed level in 2021 and, through the smoothing, the estimated slope.
Choice of intervention shape. The decay, pulses and step were chosen by looking at the data, so there is a risk of over-fitting the shape of the shock to this series. The pulse months were picked by eye.
Confounding with the exchange rate. The rand depreciated sharply in March and April 2020, at the same time as the lockdown, so the exchange rate effect is estimated mainly from the non-COVID months. It also enters without a lag, although foreign visitors book weeks or months ahead.
Profile likelihood standard errors. Treating \(\hat\delta\) as known when computing the other standard errors understates their uncertainty.
Cross-validation shortcuts. The regression’s \(\delta\) and error orders, and the ETS forms, were held fixed across origins, which favours them slightly because they were chosen with the full training set.

title: Project 3: Time Series Regression and Exponential Smoothing for South African Accommodation Demand
text:
7.3 What I would do differently
I would use multiple imputation for the COVID window so that the exponential smoothing intervals reflect the uncertainty in the imputed values, estimate \(\delta\) jointly with the other regression parameters by maximising the likelihood directly, and try a lagged exchange rate. A cleaner solution to both problems is a model that can skip the missing months without imputing them and that has the regression and smoothing ideas built in, which is what the state space models in Project 4 provide.

title: Project 3: Time Series Regression and Exponential Smoothing for South African Accommodation Demand
text:
7.4 Reflection and model development
Project 1 left me with one clear problem: the COVID collapse was the biggest obstacle to forecasting accommodation demand, and the best I could do with SARIMA was to treat those 25 months as missing. That felt unsatisfying, because those months contain real information about how demand behaves under a shock. Section 2 of the course introduced two approaches that handle this very differently, time series regression and exponential smoothing, so I wanted to see whether modelling the shock, rather than deleting it, would give better forecasts or at least a better understanding of what happened. Adding the exchange rate was a natural extension, since it linked the project to the rand I was modelling in Project 2.
The project changed shape considerably along the way. My first versions were framed around “modelling the COVID shock” and combined a single ETS model, a regression with intervention terms and a basic structural model fitted with the Kalman filter. As the portfolio came together, I realised this mixed topics from different parts of the course, and that the state space material belonged in Project 4, where it could be developed properly. I refocused this project on regression and exponential smoothing alone, which gave me room to go much deeper into each one. It also let me address a weakness I had listed in my own earlier draft, that everything rested on a single test set, by adding rolling-origin cross-validation.
On the regression side, I deliberately started with the simplest possible model, a static regression with a trend, seasonal dummies and intervention terms. Its adjusted \(R^2\) of 0.965 looked excellent, but the residuals drifted in long runs and the Durbin–Watson statistic was 0.53. That was the moment the lectures’ warning about regression on time series became concrete for me: a good in-sample fit can hide errors that make every standard error and interval unreliable. Letting the errors follow an ARIMA process fixed this, and each remaining decision came from the data. I replaced the deterministic trend with a first difference because the post-COVID level clearly did not follow a straight line. I kept seasonal dummies rather than Fourier terms because the sharp December peak needs many harmonics, which AICc confirmed. And because the decay rate enters the model non-linearly, I chose it by profiling the AICc over a grid. The most subtle lesson was in interpreting the result. With a unit root in the errors, the level shift coefficient is not the gap between the pre- and post-COVID levels, because part of the recovery is carried by the error process. I only understood this properly once the imputation regression gave a very different estimate of that gap.
Exponential smoothing taught me the opposite lesson about COVID. Fitted to the raw data, the level smoothing parameter went straight to 1, and on the log scale the model even dropped the seasonal component altogether. Unlike ARIMA, exponential smoothing cannot skip missing months, so I had to decide what to put in the gap. I chose to impute the window with a regression fitted only to the non-COVID months, which carries the seasonal pattern across the gap with a smooth transition between the two levels. Writing the Holt–Winters recursions myself was the most useful part of this section. It reproduced ETS() almost exactly, and it showed me something I would have missed by only calling the function: the 13 initial states are parameters too, and they dominate the estimation.
The results did not always agree with each other, and working out why was the most valuable part of the project. AICc preferred the undamped Holt–Winters model, but on the test set it was one of the worst, because it extrapolated a fixed downward slope for two full years, while the damped version, which lets the slope fade, was the best model of all. The test set and the cross-validation also disagreed: damped Holt–Winters won on the test set, but the Project 1 SARIMA won in cross-validation. This showed me that in-sample criteria measure one-step fit, while forecasting over two years depends mostly on how the trend is extrapolated, and that a single test set is not enough to rank models. The exchange rate gave a similar lesson. Its elasticity was insignificant, and using the actual exchange rate made the forecasts worse, because the rand strengthened over the test period while demand rose. A regression’s forecasts are only as good as the stability of the relationships it relies on.
I also tested an idea of my own. Since exponential smoothing already puts most of its weight on recent observations, I wondered whether the imputation was needed at all, or whether I could simply fit the models to the post-COVID years from April 2022. Working through it showed me that the weighting only applies to the level: in my models the seasonal pattern and the slope barely update, so they still come from the start of the series in 2015. Fitting only the last two years was the way to let them reflect current behaviour, at the cost of having just 27 months of data. The results were mixed. The undamped Holt–Winters model improved a great deal, because it no longer extrapolated a slope from 2015, but the no-trend model got worse. The damped model gave almost the same accuracy on both windows, which convinced me more than any single score that damping is the safest choice when the trend is uncertain. The seasonal pattern learned from two years was also very close to the one from the full series, which confirmed again how stable it is. In the end I kept the imputed series as the main approach, because with so little data the outcome depended too much on which trend I happened to choose.
Going forward, the main weakness I would address is that the imputed COVID months are treated as exact data. They contain no noise, which makes the exponential smoothing intervals too narrow; multiple imputation would fix this. More fundamentally, both approaches in this project needed a workaround for the missing months, either intervention terms or imputation. A state space model can skip missing observations directly while keeping the regression and smoothing ideas built in, which is exactly what Project 4 takes up.

title: TS Intro
text:
Overview of the key concepts
A time series is a set of observations indexed by time, where the order matters and neighbouring values are usually related. Before any modelling, the data have to be stored in a form that R recognises as a time series, so that it knows the spacing of the observations and where each one falls in the seasonal cycle.
The ts class. A ts object is a numeric vector with three extra attributes: start, end and frequency. The frequency is the number of observations per cycle (12 for monthly data with a yearly cycle, 4 for quarterly, 52 for weekly). start = c(2021, 1) means period 1 of 2021, so for monthly data January 2021. Periods are numbered from 1, and the second element of start can never exceed the frequency. Once these attributes are set, functions such as window(), lag(), diff(), cycle() and decompose() all know how the data are spaced.
Aggregation. Data are often collected at a finer resolution than we want to model. Daily sales can be summed to monthly totals or averaged to weekly means. The choice of resolution decides which patterns are visible: daily data show a weekly cycle and a yearly cycle, while monthly totals hide the weekly cycle completely.
Lags and differences. The lag operator shifts a series in time, \(BY_t = Y_{t-1}\). Differencing removes structure: the first difference \(\nabla Y_t = Y_t - Y_{t-1}\) removes a linear trend, and the seasonal difference \(\nabla_{12} Y_t = Y_t - Y_{t-12}\) removes a stable 12-month pattern. These are the building blocks of ARIMA and SARIMA models later in the section.
Decomposition. An additive decomposition writes the series as
\[
Y_t = T_t + S_t + R_t,
\]
a trend-cycle \(T_t\), a seasonal component \(S_t\) that repeats every \(m\) periods and sums to zero over a cycle, and a remainder \(R_t\). Classical decomposition estimates the trend with a centred moving average, then averages the detrended values for each season. STL does the same job with local regression (loess), lets the seasonal pattern change slowly over time, and is more robust to outliers.
The tidy toolkit. A tsibble is a data frame with an explicit index (the time variable) and key (which series each row belongs to), so many series can live in one table. It also distinguishes implicit gaps (missing rows) from explicit missing values (rows containing NA). feasts provides seasonal plots, ACFs, STL and feature extraction on tsibbles, and timetk produces similar diagnostics directly from an ordinary tibble.

Question 7: What is wrong with each call?
Q1. ts(x, start = c(2023, 13), frequency = 12) Monthly data have only 12 periods per year, so the second element of start cannot exceed 12. “Period 13 of 2023” does not exist; it should roll over to January 2024. Fix: ts(x, start = c(2024, 1), frequency = 12).
Q2. ts(x, start = 2023, frequency = 12) For sub-annual data (frequency > 1), start should give both the year and the period within the year. A single number is ambiguous. Fix: ts(x, start = c(2023, 1), frequency = 12).
Q3. ts(x, start = c(2023, 0), frequency = 12) Periods are numbered from 1, so period 0 does not exist; January is period 1. Fix: ts(x, start = c(2023, 1), frequency = 12).
Q4. ts(x, start = c(2023, 2), frequency = 4) “Period 2” depends on the frequency: with frequency = 4 it means Q2, not February. If the data are monthly, the frequency must match their real spacing. Fix: ts(x, start = c(2023, 2), frequency = 12).
Q5. ts(x, start = c(2023, 1), frequency = 12.5) The frequency counts observations per cycle, so it should be a whole number. Most methods built on ts objects (seasonal differencing, decompose(), seasonal ARIMA) need an integer frequency. Fix: ts(x, start = c(2023, 1), frequency = 12).
Q6. ts(x, start = c(2023, 1), frequency = 12, deltat = 1/12) frequency and deltat describe the same thing from two directions (deltat = 1/frequency), so giving both is redundant. Fix: give only one, e.g. ts(x, start = c(2023, 1), frequency = 12).
Q7. ts(x, start = c(2023, 1), frequency = 365) frequency = 365 declares daily data. If x holds monthly values, every value is placed at the wrong point in the yearly cycle. Fix: ts(x, start = c(2023, 1), frequency = 12).
Q8. window(x, start = c(2023, 13)) window() can only extract periods that exist inside the series’ range, and month 13 does not exist. Fix: start at a valid point inside the series, e.g. window(x, start = c(2024, 1)).
Q9. decompose(ts(x, frequency = 1)) With frequency = 1 there is no seasonal cycle, so there is no seasonal component to estimate. decompose() also needs at least two complete cycles. Fix: use the series’ real seasonal frequency, e.g. decompose(ts(x, frequency = 12)).

title: TS Intro
text:
Implementation in R
To understand what decompose() is doing, I wrote the classical additive decomposition from first principles and checked it against the built-in function on the monthly S001 series.

Trend. With an even period \(m = 12\), a plain 12-term moving average is not centred on a month. A \(2 \times 12\) moving average fixes this: it is a 13-term weighted average with weights \(\tfrac{1}{24}\) on the two end months and \(\tfrac{1}{12}\) on the 11 in between, \[
\hat T_t = \frac{1}{12}\left(\tfrac{1}{2}Y_{t-6} + Y_{t-5} + \dots + Y_{t+5} + \tfrac{1}{2}Y_{t+6}\right).
\] The first and last six months have no trend estimate.
Seasonal component. Detrend, \(Y_t - \hat T_t\), average the detrended values for each calendar month, then centre the 12 averages so they sum to zero.
Remainder. \(\hat R_t = Y_t - \hat T_t - \hat S_t\).



Code
my_decompose <- function(y) {
  m <- frequency(y)
  w <- if (m %% 2 == 0) c(0.5, rep(1, m - 1), 0.5) / m else rep(1, m) / m
  trend <- stats::filter(y, w, sides = 2)

  detrended <- y - trend
  s_means <- tapply(detrended, cycle(y), mean, na.rm = TRUE)
  s_means <- s_means - mean(s_means)            # seasonal effects sum to zero
  seasonal <- ts(s_means[cycle(y)], start = start(y), frequency = m)

  list(trend = trend, seasonal = seasonal, random = y - trend - seasonal,
       figure = s_means)
}

built <- decompose(sales_ts)

max_diff <- c(
  Trend     = max(abs(mine$trend    - built$trend),    na.rm = TRUE),
  Seasonal  = max(abs(mine$seasonal - built$seasonal), na.rm = TRUE),
  Remainder = max(abs(mine$random   - built$random),   na.rm = TRUE)
)

title: TS Intro
text:
Reflection
What was most challenging: Keeping track of the different ways R represents time. A ts object stores time as decimal years with a frequency attribute, a Date column stores calendar dates, and a tsibble uses an index and key. Each has its own rules: start periods are numbered from 1, frequency must match the real spacing of the data, and daily data need the seasonal period stated explicitly because there is more than one cycle. The lag() clash was the most confusing. stats::lag() shifts the time attribute while dplyr::lag() shifts the values, and which one runs depends on which packages are loaded.
What I now understand: Getting the structure of a time series right is part of the analysis, not a preliminary step. The frequency decides what cycle(), seasonal differencing and decomposition do, so a wrong frequency produces output that looks plausible but is meaningless (as in Question 7). Aggregation is a modelling choice too: summing to monthly removes the weekly cycle entirely. The difference between implicit gaps and explicit NAs in a tsibble explained why filling gaps has to happen before aggregating.
Advantages and limitations of the methods:

Advantages: Base ts objects are simple and are what most classical functions (arima, decompose, HoltWinters) expect. The tidy tools handle many series at once through the key, deal with irregular dates and gaps explicitly, and make seasonal plots for multiple periods easy.
Limitations: A ts object supports only one regular frequency, so it cannot represent daily data with both weekly and yearly cycles. Classical decomposition assumes a fixed seasonal pattern and loses the trend at the ends of the series. Filling missing days with a store mean is convenient for exploration but would bias any model fitted afterwards.

Links: Project 1 (ARIMA and SARIMA on tourism nights sold) builds on these tools, starting from a monthly ts object, a time plot, a seasonal subseries plot and an STL decomposition before differencing. See also the Week 1 journal entry.

title: ARCH and GARCH Lab
text:
Overview of the key concepts
Financial and interest-rate series share a few stylised facts: the series itself (or its changes) shows little autocorrelation, but its squares or absolute values are strongly autocorrelated. This is volatility clustering: large moves follow large moves and calm follows calm. Returns are also heavier-tailed than a normal distribution.
An ARMA model only describes the conditional mean, and assumes a constant variance. ARCH and GARCH models add an equation for the conditional variance:
\[
\varepsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t, \qquad z_t \overset{iid}{\sim} (0,1)
\]

ARCH(1): \(\sigma_t^2 = \omega + \alpha_1 \varepsilon_{t-1}^2\). Today’s variance depends on yesterday’s squared shock.
GARCH(1,1): \(\sigma_t^2 = \omega + \alpha_1 \varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta_1 \sigma_{t-1}^2\). Adding the lagged variance gives long memory in volatility with only one extra parameter. Persistence is measured by \(\alpha_1 + \beta_1\); the variance is covariance-stationary only if this is below 1.

In practice the two are combined: an ARMA model for the mean with GARCH errors, estimated jointly by maximum likelihood. The conditional distribution of \(z_t\) can be normal or a standardised \(t\) to allow fat tails.
Diagnostics work on two kinds of residuals. The raw residuals \(\hat\varepsilon_t\) still contain the changing variance, so the ACF of \(\hat\varepsilon_t^2\) shows whether ARCH effects are present. The standardised residuals \(\hat z_t = \hat\varepsilon_t / \hat\sigma_t\) should be white noise with no remaining structure in their squares if the model is adequate. Ljung-Box tests on \(\hat z_t\) and \(\hat z_t^2\) formalise this.
A fitted GARCH model gives a conditional forecast distribution for the next observation, which lets us compute probabilities of extreme moves given yesterday’s information. This is the basis of Value-at-Risk.

(a) acf(res) plots the sample autocorrelations of the raw residuals \(\hat\varepsilon_t = Y_t - \hat\mu - \widehat{\text{ar1}}\, Y_{t-1}\). It checks the mean equation. Almost all lags lie within the bounds; lag 2 is borderline (-0.14) and the Ljung-Box p-value is 0.075. The AR(1) mean is adequate, though only just at the 10% level.
(b) acf(res^2) plots the autocorrelations of the squared raw residuals. These are still strongly autocorrelated (lag 4 is 0.55; Ljung-Box p < 0.001). This is not a sign of poor fit. The raw residuals are \(\sigma_t z_t\), so they still carry the time-varying variance by construction. The plot tells us that GARCH effects are present in the series, which is the reason for modelling the variance.
(c) acf(res_std^2) plots the autocorrelations of the squared standardised residuals \(\hat z_t^2 = (\hat\varepsilon_t / \hat\sigma_t)^2\). If the variance equation has captured the clustering, these should be white noise. They nearly are: the largest spike is lag 4 (0.16) and the Ljung-Box p-value is 0.273. (d) garch.model.Tbill@sigma.t holds the fitted conditional standard deviations \(\hat\sigma_t = \sqrt{\hat\omega + \hat\alpha_1 \hat\varepsilon_{t-1}^2}\), one per quarter. They range from 0.58 to 3.86. Dividing the residuals by them gives the standardised residuals.

With \(\hat\mu_t\) = -0.0032, \(\hat\sigma_t\) = 0.0171 and \(\hat\nu\) = 4.11, the conditional probability is 2.11e-05. That is about once every 188 years of trading days. Black Monday was 13.2 conditional standard deviations below the forecast mean.
Two observations. First, the GARCH model had already raised the forecast volatility to 1.7 times the two-year sample standard deviation, because the preceding week (including a -5.4% fall on the Friday) was turbulent. Second, the heavy tails matter enormously: under a normal distribution with the same mean and standard deviation the probability would be 5.3e-40, i.e. effectively impossible.

A model that fits well in sample still gave Black Monday a tiny probability: good diagnostics do not protect against rare events outside the data’s experience.

title: ARCH and GARCH Lab
text:
Implementation in R
To understand what garchFit is doing, I wrote the AR(1)/ARCH(1) Gaussian log-likelihood myself and maximised it with optim, using the Del.Tbill data from Part A.
For \(t = 2, \dots, n\), with \(\varepsilon_t = (Y_t - m) - \phi (Y_{t-1} - m)\) and \(\sigma_t^2 = \omega + \alpha_1 \varepsilon_{t-1}^2\):
\[
\ell(m, \phi, \omega, \alpha_1) = -\frac{1}{2}\sum_t \left[\log(2\pi) + \log\sigma_t^2 + \frac{\varepsilon_t^2}{\sigma_t^2}\right].
\]
I parametrise with the mean \(m\) (not the intercept), and optimise over \(\log\omega\) and \(\text{logit}(\alpha_1)\), so that \(\omega > 0\) and \(0 < \alpha_1 < 1\) hold automatically. The recursion starts with \(\sigma_1^2\) equal to the sample variance.


Code
arch1_nll <- function(theta, y) {
  m <- theta[1]; phi <- theta[2]
  omega <- exp(theta[3]); alpha <- plogis(theta[4])
  n <- length(y)
  e <- numeric(n)
  e[1] <- y[1] - m
  e[-1] <- (y[-1] - m) - phi * (y[-n] - m)
  s2 <- numeric(n); s2[1] <- var(y)
  for (t in 2:n) s2[t] <- omega + alpha * e[t - 1]^2
  -sum(dnorm(e, 0, sqrt(s2), log = TRUE))
}

y <- as.numeric(Del.Tbill)
own <- optim(c(mean(y), 0.2, log(var(y) / 2), 0), arch1_nll, y = y, method = "BFGS")
own_est <- c(mean = own$par[1], ar1 = own$par[2],
             omega = exp(own$par[3]), alpha1 = plogis(own$par[4]))

fg <- coef(garch.model.Tbill)
compare <- rbind(
  "Own MLE" = c(own_est, `-logL` = own$value),
  "fGarch"  = c(mean = unname(fg["mu"] / (1 - fg["ar1"])), fg[c("ar1", "omega", "alpha1")],
                `-logL` = garch.model.Tbill@fit$llh))

title: ARCH and GARCH Lab
text:
Reflection
What was most challenging: Reading the fGarch output correctly. Three things caught me out: mu is the intercept rather than the mean, the AIC from summary() is divided by the sample size (so it cannot be compared with arima() until multiplied by \(n\)), and "std" is a \(t\) rescaled to unit variance, so the probability in Part B needs the \(\sqrt{(\nu-2)/\nu}\) correction if computed with pt(). Understanding the different jobs of raw and standardised residuals also took time: significant autocorrelation in res^2 is expected, while the same in res_std^2 would mean the model has failed.
What I now understand: A GARCH model is a model for the conditional variance, and its value shows up in conditional statements, such as the probability of a crash given yesterday’s information. Transformations matter as much as model choice. On the raw T-bill changes, a GARCH(1,1) produced an explosive variance because volatility was tied to the level of rates; on log changes the same model gave stationary, sensible persistence. Choosing the right scale for the data fixed a problem that no extra GARCH term could. I also saw that the conditional distribution is not a detail: with the same mean and volatility forecast, the \(t\) and normal assumptions gave Black Monday probabilities about 35 orders of magnitude apart.
Advantages and limitations of the methods:

Advantages: GARCH models capture volatility clustering with few parameters, give one-step-ahead volatility forecasts and conditional probabilities directly, and combine naturally with an ARMA mean. With \(t\) errors they also allow for fat tails.
Limitations: Variance responds only to the size of past shocks, not to their sign or to the level of the series (the level effect in T-bill rates needed a transformation instead). The model is symmetric, so it cannot capture the leverage effect where falls raise volatility more than rises (GJR-GARCH or EGARCH would). Good in-sample diagnostics say nothing about events outside the sample’s experience: the Black Monday model passed every check yet still put the crash at roughly a once-in-two-centuries event. Model choice between ARCH and GARCH can also be ambiguous when AIC and BIC disagree, as in Part B (c).

Links: Project 2 (USD/ZAR volatility and VaR backtesting) extends this lab to daily exchange-rate returns, with my own GARCH likelihood, GJR-GARCH and rolling VaR backtests. See also the journal entry for the ARCH/GARCH week.
